JetBlue Adds Fresh Destination in Latin America, Caribbean Expansion

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (273 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Airlinegeeks

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • JetBlue is growing its presence in Central America and the Caribbean.
  • For the first time ever, the carrier will serve the Honduran capital of Tegucigalpa.
  • Currently, JetBlue’s only destination in Honduras is San Pedro Sula, in the country’s northwest.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

JetBlue is growing its presence in Central America and the Caribbean.

For the first time ever, the carrier will serve the Honduran capital of Tegucigalpa. Starting Feb. 25, 2027, flights from Fort Lauderdale, Florida, will arrive at Palmerola International Airport in Comayagua, which serves Tegucigalpa.

Currently, JetBlue’s only destination in Honduras is San Pedro Sula, in the country’s northwest.

In a recent development, on Feb. 23, the carrier will launch service between Fort Lauderdale and George Town, Grand Cayman, in the Cayman Islands.

Both routes will operate daily, using a mix of Airbus A320 and A220 aircraft.

In a recent development, jetBlue will also offer limited-time daily service from Fort Lauderdale to Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago, between Jan. 29 and Feb. 15. The connection will help travelers reach the islands during Carnival, the airline noted.

Sources indicate that “We’re grateful for the way customers across South Florida continue to embrace JetBlue, and we’re committed to delivering even more of the destinations and travel options they’re looking for,” Daniel Shurz, JetBlue’s senior vice president of revenue, network, and enterprise planning, mentioned in a news release. “With newly introduced international service to Honduras and Grand Cayman, we’re strengthening Fort Lauderdale’s role as a key gateway to Latin America and the Caribbean, making it easier for customers to reconnect with loved ones, explore new places, and travel across our growing network.”.

According to recent reports, american has prioritized Latin America as demand from U.S. markets, especially Miami, grows. The carrier just recently released service to Barranquilla and Cali in Colombia and will add Barcelona, Venezuela, to its network in January.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally introduced a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E.
  • In a recent development, the lame-duck session continues as lawmakers look ahead to Thanksgiving and the funding deadline that arrives in December.
  • Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally debuted a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally introduced a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

In a recent development, the lame-duck session continues as lawmakers look ahead to Thanksgiving and the funding deadline that arrives in December. The primary legislative business this week is the Senate's bipartisan permitting overhaul, but a late-breaking aviation funding fight and the Senate Democratic leadership contest are also commanding attention.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally debuted a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., and both men are accumulating supporters ahead of leadership votes that are presently scheduled for early December — though there's been an effort to move that up to this week.

Van Hollen has expressed disagreement with Schumer's participation in primaries.

​"I don't think it's the role of the Senate majority leader to get involved in open, contested Democratic primaries," Van Hollen said Sunday on CNN.

According to recent reports, ​Van Hollen has also remarked he wants to use all available tools to stop funding for the Iran war immediately, with a government funding deadline in December. That's going to be one of several flash points for December's funding discussions, as President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans try to use what leverage they have before Democrats take the gavels in the House and the Senate in January.

A upcoming concern is the state of federal air traffic control after Friday's nationwide ground stop, with the Trump administration now seeking $50 billion to upgrade systems.

"I need additional money to do the additional work to keep the airspace safe," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy remarked on Fox News Sunday.

Industry observers note that sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, a senior appropriator who is in line to become majority whip, has suggested reallocating funds from the additional money the Trump administration and congressional Republicans allocated to Immigration and Customs Enforcement to address the challenges at the Federal Aviation Administration.

It has been revealed that "There is a pot of 60 billion extra dollars on top of the regularly appropriated amount for ICE and we should use at least a portion of that money for the FAA. We can solve this problem and not spend any additional taxpayer dollars," Schatz posted on X.

In a recent development, "We can do all things, we don't have to do one versus the other," Duffy said in the Fox News Sunday interview. "I don't think that is the answer. The answer is let's do everything that's going to keep Americans safe, whether it's with immigration or it's with air travel.".

Meanwhile on the Senate floor, the energy permitting overhaul bill faces a key test Monday evening​, with a vote scheduled to limit debate on a substitute amendment that represents the most recent version of the bill. Votes on a number of President Donald Trump's judicial nominations are also lined up this week.

It has been revealed that on the other side of the Capitol, the House floor schedule i​ncludes several labor-related bills. ​One of the measures, introduced by Sen.-elect Kevin Hern, R-Okla.,​ would set standards for the way labor law applies to franchise operators.

New member orientation is also continuing, and committees in both the House and Senate will be holding hearings throughout the week as the outgoing Republican committee chairs aim to get through priority items on their agenda before the end of the Congress.

According to recent reports, that includes a Tuesday morning Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing for Hung Cao, the nominee to be Navy secretary, who is right now the acting secretary. The Senate Judiciary Committee will be busy as well, as Chairman Charles E. Grassley, R-Iowa, looks to tee up more of Trump's judicial nominations for floor consideration.

Booking travel often means navigating fixed prices on flights, hotels, and car rentals—but Priceline has been finding ways around that since 1999. From up to 40% off in the Cyber Week sale to 60% off Hotel Express Deals to up to 20% off rental cars and 50% off flights, these Priceline coupons can leave a little more room in the budget for the parts of the trip I'll actually remember.

In a recent development, the best time to book a getaway might just be before everyone else starts shopping. It's just about that time, and Priceline is giving its VIP members a head start on its Cyber Week Early Access sale, running now through November 23, 2026, at 9 a.m. ET. The weeklong promotion lets members save up to 40% on eligible hotel stays, plus additional deals across flights, rental cars, vacation packages, cruises, and experiences.

No coupon code is needed to unlock the early-access offers; simply sign in to your free Priceline VIP account to browse qualifying deals. Not a member yet? Joining is free, so you can get in on the savings before the sale opens to everyone on November 23. The main Cyber Week sale runs through December 2, with additional Black Friday, Cyber Monday, and Travel Tuesday flash deals on the calendar.

Recent findings suggest that if you book through Priceline regularly, it's worth signing up for the free Priceline VIP rewards program. Unlike traditional hotel loyalty programs, Priceline VIP rewards your overall booking activity across hotels, rental cars, and more, with each tier unlocking deeper discounts and extra perks.

Compared with other online travel booking rewards programs—such as those from Hotels.com, Vrbo, and Booking.com—Priceline's VIP program stands out for rewarding bookings across multiple travel categories rather than focusing primarily on accommodations, making it a useful option if you regularly bundle different parts of your trip. (Trust me, it's worth it.).

You don't necessarily need a promo code to save on Priceline. Rather its general Deals page rounds up various ways to spend less, including vacation bundles that can save you up to 55% when you combine flights, hotels, and rental cars in one single booking. You can also find deals on popular destinations and up to 20% off featured rental car brands, making it always worth checking the page before you book.

For an even bigger discount—and a little more mystery—try Priceline's Express Deals. These offers let you choose your travel dates, destination, preferred star rating, amenities, and price range, but keep the hotel name and exact location hidden until after you book. In exchange for that element of surprise, Priceline can offer significantly discounted rates, with significant savings of up to 60%.

Industry observers note that that said, these fun Express Deals are best for flexible travelers who aren't set on a specific hotel and would rather save than know every detail upfront. The same concept can apply to flights and other travel bookings featured through Priceline's Express Deals offerings, though the exact discounts and availability vary. One important catch: Express Deals are non-refundable, so take note of that prior to booking.

It has been revealed that priceline also offers VIP Deals, which are exclusive offers and benefits for rewards members. Sign in to your Priceline account to see which VIP savings are available to you.

According to recent reports, express Deals and VIP Deals offer great savings, but they work a bit differently: Express Deals offer up to a 60% discount automatically on rental car companies, hotels, and flight carriers—but the catch is that you won't know the hotel name until after you book. It's a bit of a mystery with a surprise element attached: travelers select ideal travel dates, location, and general preferences such as star rating, amenities, or price range, but the hotel name and exact location remain hidden until after you book. This allows Priceline to offer you a discounted rate, as hotels can fill their rooms without publicly lowering their prices.

It has been revealed that on that note, Express Deals are ideal for travelers who are flexible and open to a bit of mystery in exchange for significant savings. It's a great option if you're not set on a specific hotel and are willing to take a chance on where you'll stay, and for those who value savings over knowing every detail upfront. Though do note, Express Deals are non-refundable. VIP Deals, on the other hand, are exclusive offers available to rewards members, with some discounts and benefits that aren't available to regular users. To view these deals, make sure you're signed into your Priceline account.

Priceline has partnered with the American Forces Travel (AFT) to offer up to an extra 50% off travel with pre-negotiated rates on flights and hotels. The AFT, supported by Priceline, is the US Department of Defense's official online leisure travel site for active military, Guard or Reserve, US Coast Guard, retired military, and all eligible MWR patrons. Check if you're eligible and complete their authentication process to save on your next trip.

For your easy reference, there are a few things you’ll want to know before you check out. Priceline promo codes usually have capped discount values, but the brand frequently offers discounts of around $50 or $75 off for hotels, as well as up to $625 off flight and hotel coupons for bundle deals. The most frequent promo codes are for the site’s hotel Express Deals, and new offers are typically released around two to three times per month.

According to recent reports, if your Priceline promo code isn't working, don't assume it's invalid and give up—most codes come with a handful of restrictions. Double-check that the code hasn't expired, that it's valid for the type of booking you're making, and that you've met any minimum spend or eligibility requirements. Some discounts apply only to Express Deals, while others are limited to hotels, rental cars, or select flights, and many can't be combined with another promotion or automatically discounted rate.

It's also worth quickly confirming that you're signed in to the correct Priceline account, especially if you're trying to redeem a VIP-exclusive offer, as many member discounts are tied to your account rather than available at checkout for everyone. If everything looks right and the code still won't apply, removing and re-adding your booking or trying a different browser or device can sometimes resolve the temporary concern. And if all else fails, Priceline's customer support can confirm whether the promotion is still active or help identify why it isn't applying to your reservation.

Biden: ‘Hard to take’ as Pelosi, Schumer turned on him in 2024

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1363 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, president Joe Biden, Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., arrive for The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 bill signing at the White House, on Aug.
  • It has been revealed that in conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir.
  • Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, president Joe Biden, Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., arrive for The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 bill signing at the White House, on Aug. 9, 2022. In his upcoming memoir, Biden said he was disappointed when Pelosi and Schumer urged him to drop out of the presidential race in 2024. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

It has been revealed that in conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir. The consensus view, even among some who’d worked for the former president, was that if he did anything other than accept some responsibility for his role in Donald Trump’s return to the White House, they didn’t have much appetite to hear what he had to say about anything else.

Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.

But while his perspective on the climactic moment of his political career will be the most scrutinized portion of Biden’s fresh book, “Promise Me, America” seems primarily intended to offer the former president a platform he has otherwise not had since leaving office: to catalog what he sees as his historic achievements and offer his perspective on how he wrestled with the major concerns of our time.

It’s often said that the only thing better than being president is being a former president. That has hardly been the case for Biden in the nearly 22 months since he left the White House, especially as he’s endured what his son Hunter has described as “debilitating” physical pain following a cancer diagnosis last March.

But where “Thanks, Obama” became a popular mantra nearly a decade ago for Democrats seeking to defend and celebrate the 44th president’s record in contrast with the first Trump administration, no such widespread nostalgia has emerged around Biden, as the party is loath to revisit the trauma of the summer of 2024.

Recent findings suggest that the sheer length of his new book — more than 400 pages — seems an implicit acknowledgment that presenting a positive portrait of Biden’s single term in office is largely to be a solitary effort. Over 15 chapters, Biden offers sometimes mechanical descriptions of specific policies and their impact, but also new details of the sausage-making required to pass major initiatives like the Inflation Reduction Act. That legislation, he writes, was revived thanks in part to an Italian dinner hosted by Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo to make peace between West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin III and White House Chief of Staff Ron Klain.

Biden writes in sweeping terms about other accomplishments like responding to the COVID-19 crisis he inherited, calling his administration’s work “one of the most monumental achievements in public health history.” He repeatedly defends his frequent efforts to warn Americans about the need to safeguard our democracy even as critics in the press and his own party suggested he focus more on economic concerns.

Supporting Ukraine in its war against Russia gets the most extensive treatment of any single matter in the book, including a detailed account of Biden’s clandestine trip to Kyiv in February 2023. And the former Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman takes great effort to delve into the complexity of the U.S.-China relationship and his relationship with President Xi Jinping, while asserting that Taiwan “will likely be the most important foreign policy challenge in the world over the next generation.”.

In a recent development, recurring throughout the book are expressions of optimism that under his administration, Washington was beginning to work again like it was supposed to, that America’s global leadership was being restored through its alliances, and that he was tackling problems that previous presidents had sidestepped. And in offering this comprehensive presentation of his record, Biden also offers his primary rationale for running again.

Recent findings suggest that “We had accomplished so much —  I wanted to finish the job. And yes: I believed I was the best person to do it,” he claims. “I was the only person who had ever beaten Donald Trump. And I felt I was the best person to do it again.”.

It has been revealed that one of Biden’s top advisers put it to me a different way in the months leading up to his decision to seek another term. “He has been running for president for 50 years. And the idea that he would actually be president and stop running for president is almost laughably preposterous.”.

The biggest question, of course, was his age, something Biden, who was 81 when he dropped out of the race, asserts he gave serious consideration.

Sources indicate that “I knew better than anyone how old I was. I knew what I was —  and wasn’t —  capable of doing. I carefully monitored how I was meeting the demands of the job. And there is not a single example of me failing to handle my responsibilities,” he writes.

The June 27 debate, of course, created a very different perception, as Biden acknowledges that his flubbed comment that “we finally beat Medicare” was to become “Exhibit A that I was too old to do the job.” But he tries to argue it was no different than the poor showings of previous incumbent presidents, including President Barack Obama, in their first debates.

According to recent reports, “The difference was that every other president was given the chance to redeem themselves in a second debate. As it turned out, that chance would not be available to me,” Biden writes.

He argues the response he was seeing from voters at his public events after the debate didn’t justify the panicked response of elected Democrats in Washington, and that public polling demonstrated only minor slippage after the debate, until a steady drumbeat of elected Democrats publicly began calling for him to step aside.

Recent findings suggest that describing separate visits from former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., personally urging him to step aside, he says there was a “yawning gap between what I was seeing with Democratic voters and what I was hearing from the Democratic leadership in Washington.”.

It has been revealed that “I have to admit it was personally hard to take so many old friends turning on me,” Biden notes. “I told Schumer he had a lot of gumption (I may have said it differently at the time), coming to my home and telling me to get out of the race. Loyalty matters to me. If I give you my word, I stick with you. If I say I’m with you, I’m with you to the end.”.

At one point, Biden seems to reflect some resentment that some of the Democrats who would ultimately call on him to drop out of the race had themselves been too afraid to challenge him in the first place, saying: “Anyone who was scared off from running has no business being president.” While there was a constant narrative about the weakness of his candidacy, Biden acknowledges, the lack of a serious challenger was in fact a sign of his strength.

“I had it on good authority that several big names in Democratic politics had looked at running. They held meetings and took polls and talked to donors and to potential staff. If they thought I was weak or vulnerable, they would have taken their shot. But they didn’t,” he writes.

Industry observers note that biden’s defiant tone, and his insistence that the lack of party unity was a greater threat to his continued candidacy than his own performance, may be dismissed by Democrats who don’t want to revisit this difficult chapter. But as Schumer and other Democratic leaders are now facing their own internal challenges, “Promise Me, America” may also serve as a cautionary note for an ambitious crop of potential candidates hoping to reclaim the presidency in 2028.

On Tour: Australian Indie Darling Radio Free Alice on Tour Life, Guerrilla Gigs, and American Motels

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1770 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This article is part of a newly introduced series, On Tour, in which we talk to touring artists about life on the road.
  • Industry observers note that on Halloween, a bouncing crowd of skateboarders, witches, ghosts, and ghouls slowly coalesced in Upcoming York City's Tompkins Square Park.
  • It has been revealed that that’s what makes the album title so apt: The young Aussies are caught between cities and countries, trying to make sense of everyday life while the road itself starts to feel like home.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article is part of a newly introduced series, On Tour, in which we talk to touring artists about life on the road.

Industry observers note that on Halloween, a bouncing crowd of skateboarders, witches, ghosts, and ghouls slowly coalesced in Upcoming York City's Tompkins Square Park. They were there for a quintessentially East Village pop-up concert headlined by the Melbourne-based post-punk band Radio Free Alice (followed by an after party at Niagara). The band's debut album, What’s In Between, was just released the day prior, blending the high energy of ’80s new wave with biting social satire and a healthy dose of cheek. Having picked up a following in Australia and Europe, the four-piece group has built an underground reputation on guerrilla gigs like this one—held everywhere from beneath London railway bridges and Melbourne’s former Pentridge Prison to suburban backyards in Austin, Texas.

It has been revealed that that’s what makes the album title so apt: The young Aussies are caught between cities and countries, trying to make sense of everyday life while the road itself starts to feel like home. They’re in the thick of their own coming-of-age story, and one that's unfolding on an international stage. Fresh off the first dates of a nearly sold-out European lineup, tickets are now on sale for their What's In Between North America tour, which will kick off in San Francisco on February 24, 2027.

Industry observers note that earlier this month, vocalist and guitarist Noah Learmonth picked up my call from a Sprinter van somewhere in Germany, on the road from Copenhagen to Berlin. With the wit, gumption, and on-stage vocals of a Gen-Z Morrissey, his devilish grin fills the screen as he tells me he spends 99% of his time in the window seat behind the van’s little table, facing forward. His preferred seat is currently occupied by guitarist Jules Paradiso. He gives me a 360-degree tour of their ecosystem, where everyone has settled into their own version of life on the road. Drummer Lochie Dowd has claimed a small sleeping nook near the back. Michael Phillips, bassist and resident reader, sits with his Kindle, having just finished Christos Tsiolkas’s The Slap. As for who’s running the show? “Fuck, no one,” the still-grinning Noah states. “There’s a man up front called Ben, our tour manager, who’s a crazy man. He’s the one who leads the blind. We’d all be fucked otherwise.”.

According to recent reports, what’s everyone’s travel personality on tour? Who’s running the show?

In a recent development, yeah, [I'm] type D. I’m sort of in my own world when I’m traveling—headphones on, that kind of vibe. Jules is really easy company. He’s a valuable asset to have in the world. Michael’s pretty chill, too. He’s looking at me now as I summarize his personality. Lochie likes to sleep in this little nook. That’s a big part of his tour experience: finding that little nook.

It has been revealed that when we met Ben, we just fell in love with him and his crazy methods, his madness. The thing about Ben is he gets our sound right every time. It’s really annoying when someone else does the sound and you watch the videos back and go, ‘Oh my God, what the fuck? Why is there no bass in the synth? Why do we sound like Duran Duran? What’s going on? I sound like Sonic Youth.’ That’s not at all what we were going for. Two of my favorite bands, though. But Ben gets exactly the sound we’re going for, and he’s a real empath. We’ve spent so much time on the road together. He’s our guy.

Where do you stay while you're on the road?

Recent findings suggest that when we’re touring Europe, we’ll stay in budget hotels. Either an Ibis or a Travelodge. In America, it’s more motel-type places—Motel 6 kind of things. It’s very cliché, but kind of sick in a way. Each morning when you wake up, you set your alarm for half an hour before you have to leave, get up, have a shower, smash your clothes into your backpack, and run down to the lobby so you’re not late and Ben doesn’t give you a verbal spanking.

It has been revealed that terrible. I just had McDonald’s. I don’t even like McDonald’s. You literally don’t have an option. You pull into a service station and the only food there is McDonald’s. Jules is a Big Mac guy, though. I know that.

I’m personally notoriously light. I just have this yellow North Face backpack that I’ve had since I was about seven years old. My auntie gave it to me for my birthday. My trusty yellow backpack. Lochie has a significant suitcase, Michael has a smaller suitcase, and Jules has a big, backpacker-style backpack.

Essentials you can’t tour without?

I’m wearing the same jeans I’ve been wearing every day for the past year. I got them from a thrift shop in Melbourne. So my essentials are my jeans. Lochie’s are his headphones—we all use Sony. Jules’s is…video games. He’d hate that I just remarked that. Let’s say his laptop. Michael’s is his Kindle. He’s the best reader. Let’s see what he’s reading…ah, he just finished The Slap.

What's your favorite city that you've played in so far?

According to recent reports, new York. I mean, the obvious answer is New York. New York’s the best city in the fucking world. It’s amazing.

In a recent development, the first few times we were there, we partied a lot. We just mentioned, ‘This is a fucking adult amusement park.’ It’s ridiculous. We were staying with this band called Been Stellar, too, who are great. When we’re back we like going out on the Lower East Side, especially to this bar called Treasure Club. I personally also love the diners. I think the atmosphere in an old-school, family-run diner might be the best atmosphere of any place in the world.

Favorite venue you’ve ever played?

A gig is just people playing music, and it can happen literally anywhere. There are no rules. You can do it anywhere. Shaking up the gig setting—rethinking what a gig is and what it can feel like—is really fun, and it keeps it important. The Melbourne set at Pentridge Prison [a former 19th century prison that's been transformed into a residential area] was sick. It was an incredible visual.

What about a city that surprised you?

According to recent reports, zurich. So random. I just remember having a strangely amazing time. I remember leaving that gig thinking, ‘Actually, there was something incredibly awesome and sweet about that.’ And it was the people. They were just these thoughtful, sweet people.

In a recent development, after a show like Zurich, we’ll be in the green room after. We’ll probably crack open a beer, and Lochie will be funny. If it went really, really well, we might go out somewhere nearby, to a pub or a bar or something. But generally, what happens is we go back to the green room, we’re really buzzed, we’ll have a beer and we’ll be pretty hyped up. Then Ben will come in and say, ‘All hands on deck. We need to load up the van. We’ve got to get to the next city.’ Zurich, though—I’d love to do it again.

What's your impression of the United States so far?

It has been revealed that I mean, there’s one thing about America: the difference between, say, Latest York and LA, and then LA and Minneapolis or somewhere, is worlds apart. You could be in completely different countries.

In a recent development, middle America can feel like an absolute time warp. When you’re on the road, there’s a sort of repetitiveness to the long stretches of road that all seem to look exactly the same. You arrive at a petrol station that’s identical to the last one you stopped at. There’s that stereotype that Americans are major talkers, but I’ve found that’s almost underrated. I can’t believe how chatty Americans are. They love just talking, going on and on. Coming from Australia, it’s the opposite. I love it.

Any memories you've made on the road that you’ll never forget?

The first time we played in LA, this very sweet girl called Alice randomly made us all these gifts. She gave us all these handmade things: embroidered bracelets with band-related names and glasses with our names on them. I find something quite American about that. It’s just so sweet. In Europe, people tend to be a little less expressive in that way. It’s still just amazing to me.

Industry observers note that glasgow had this sort of “rara”-ness to it, which was really fun and funny for us. It just felt so boisterous. We’d play a slower song, and they’d still find a way to just absolutely lose their minds. It was cute.

When you're not on tour, where’s home for you guys?

According to recent reports, nowhere, not really anywhere. I’m not exaggerating. I feel disingenuous calling anywhere our home at this point. But if there were one, it would be London. It’s making a significant impression on us. What’s cool is that, a year before we moved to London, we played to maybe one person at one of our gigs there. Then, the following year, we played to this really big, sold-out room. It was an incredibly high-energy, adrenaline-fueled, amazing, crazy show. That was special. I’ll never forget it. It was probably my favorite show.

There are so many young indie-rock bands coming up in London that I’m seeing, and they’re all ambitious and exciting. I’m really excited by London. It’s lived up to the hopes I had for it. Because of that we’ve found ourselves hanging out at venues like the Shacklewell Arms and the George Tavern, that sort of thing.

While you're on tour, what do you miss the most?

You know, this isn’t a very cool answer, and I kind of wish it were, but the truth is I really miss having an exercise routine. In Melbourne, I was really big on swimming every morning, doing laps or going to the gym. I find it puts me in a really good place for the day. I’m chill and focused, not neurotic, and I just find it’s really good for me.

What's a band touring right now that you are personally excited about?

It has been revealed that lime Garden. They’re an all female lineup. The English rock scene is a bit of a sausage fest, so they’re a breath of fresh air.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Southwest and French Bee are joining forces to expand international travel options for passengers not only on both sides of the Atlantic, but also the Pacific.
  • The agreement connects French Bee’s international network with Southwest’s extensive domestic network in the U.S.
  • French Bee also flies to Newark, New Jersey, but Southwest does not offer service there.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Southwest and French Bee are joining forces to expand international travel options for passengers not only on both sides of the Atlantic, but also the Pacific. The two carriers announced a newly introduced interline partnership that will allow travelers to combine flights on both airlines under a single ticket.

The agreement connects French Bee’s international network with Southwest’s extensive domestic network in the U.S. The partnership will provide connections through French Bee’s three U.S. gateway airports that Southwest also serves: Los Angeles, Miami, and San Francisco.

French Bee also flies to Newark, New Jersey, but Southwest does not offer service there.

Passengers will be able to connect between French Bee’s international flights and Southwest domestic flights without having to purchase separate tickets for each airline or recheck bags at each airline.

French Bee operates an all-Airbus A350 fleet, with its primary hub located at Paris-Orly Airport, and operations to North America and destinations in the Indian Ocean and South Pacific.

Southwest passengers will gain access to French Bee destinations not only from Paris, but also Tahiti in French Polynesia, which the French carrier flies to from San Francisco. The partnership will also offer one-stop French Bee connections from Paris to the Maldives and Sri Lanka, scheduled to launch in December 2026, along with current flights to Reunion Island.

For French Bee customers, the upcoming arrangement provides access to a much larger network of domestic destinations throughout the U.S. Southwest’s network includes cities such as Las Vegas, Chicago, Dallas, Denver, Nashville, Austin, San Diego, Phoenix, and multiple destinations in the Hawaiian Islands.

The agreement represents another step in Southwest’s expanding international connectivity strategy, as the airline continues to develop relationships with overseas carriers rather than rely exclusively on its own international operations with its all-Boeing 737 fleet.

Tickets for connecting flights are now available through French Bee’s website.

#77268. Latest Update: I Walked Solo Along England’s Rugged South West Coast Path for Three Days

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1640 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: I Walked Solo Along England’s Rugged South West Coast Path for Three Days

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1640 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that I’m standing atop a spit of land jutting out into the English Channel, peering down at a beach accessible only by boat, where a small group of sunbathers lounge on the rocky sand.
  • I was nearing the end of the first day of a three-day solo walking trip along a slice of England’s South West Coast Path, a 630-mile trail through some of the country’s most beautiful land- and seascapes.
  • It has been revealed that since tackling an admittedly easier two-day walk from Dover to Sandwich the previous summer, I’d become totally enamored with England’s coastal paths.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I’m standing atop a spit of land jutting out into the English Channel, peering down at a beach accessible only by boat, where a small group of sunbathers lounge on the rocky sand. The view is a welcome excuse to catch my breath before continuing along five more rolling cliffs—400 steep feet up, 400 steep feet down, and repeat. And so, despite my exhausted legs and the blister that’s forming over my right big toe, I decide to imprint this impossibly peaceful scene into my brain to remind myself why I’m doing this trip.

Dorset's limestone Jurassic Coast.

I was nearing the end of the first day of a three-day solo walking trip along a slice of England’s South West Coast Path, a 630-mile trail through some of the country’s most beautiful land- and seascapes. Earlier this year, it became part of the newly created King Charles III England Coast Path, inaugurated with a brisk March walk by the king himself (wearing a suit, natch). The route now incorporates all of England’s preexisting regional coastal paths, adding newly introduced sections to create a wider network that stretches across nearly 2,700 miles, giving walkers a chance to access parts of the country far beyond the typical travel itinerary.

It has been revealed that since tackling an admittedly easier two-day walk from Dover to Sandwich the previous summer, I’d become totally enamored with England’s coastal paths. I realized I could experience so much more of the country’s most beautiful landscapes by foot than I ever could by train or car. For my second foray, I chose one of the more frequented set of trails: walking east from Weymouth to Bournemouth across Dorset. This stretch is known for its incredible rock formations, the result of millions of years of waves washing against the coast. That erosion has also led to the discovery of some of the world’s oldest fossils—giving the region the name of Jurassic Coast.

A view of the South West coast Path's rugged countryside, which is now more easily accessible to hikers thanks to the wider newly created King Charles III England Coast Path.

When I’d set off five hours earlier from the charming seaside town of Weymouth—a destination made popular by King George III’s multiple visits at the turn of the 19th century—the going had been easy. My only roadblock was a military parade that a British historical society couldn’t have arranged any better: an Army band marched in front of a stretch of beach-facing Georgian townhouses as Union Jack bunting fluttered in the sea breeze. An Anglican priest delivered a short prayer. There was a Spitfire flyover. If you ignored all the iPhones and mobility scooters, it was a scene that would have fit in comfortably 80 years ago.

By setting out alone on a three-day walk, I was seeking solitude, and moments like that clifftop break, when I had the view all to myself, delivered. But the long way out of the Weymouth hubbub also clarified why walking England’s coastal paths is so approachable—especially for those of us who love the outdoors but want to sleep indoors. Since the country is quite densely populated, you can easily walk the trails from town to town, and hotel to hotel, without the weight (and stress) of camping equipment. For those same reasons, it’s also perfect as a solo walker; the risks feel more manageable when you know medical care is within reach; that you’re rarely without phone service; and that your hotel door locks at night.

Recent findings suggest that after 12 miles or so of walking, I arrived at West Lulworth, a town of centuries-old stone cottages that can best be described as “quaint.” I was greeted by the famous Durdle Door, a limestone arch that snakes out of a cliff and into the Channel, with clusters of beachgoers splashing underneath. It's a place worth lingering: After going down my final descent of the day, I snuck a peek at Lulworth Cove, a popular bay almost fully enclosed by limestone (and a UNESCO World Heritage Site), before checking into the Old Barn Inn, a B&B up the road for a gloriously hot shower.

A view of Durdle Door, a limestone arch that can be seen from the trail.

My second day of walking presented a new challenge: Part of my planned route was closed because it crossed a firing range in use by the Army for training. To avoid it, I rode the bus (the Jurassic Coast is very well served by public transit, at least in summer) part of the way to my next destination, then planned to take a shortcut through some fields to get back to the coast. Sarah, the owner of the Old Barn, had given me extremely specific verbal directions based on local landmarks, which were easy enough to follow until I’d reached the “horrible hill” she warned me of. It was then that I realized I was in the middle of a field with no obvious path out. I bushwhacked to a nearby road, the peace of solitude nowhere to be found as I muttered, “I’ve done this to myself.”.

In a recent development, but thanks to my two puny bars of cell phone service, I navigated over another field, through a herd of sheep, along a ravine, and then emerged, alarmingly sweaty, into the absolutely charming limestone village of Worth Matravers. I made a beeline to the local pub (as recommended by Sarah), and enjoyed what was undoubtedly the best pint of my life looking out over a grassy field—and to the ocean beyond. As I sipped my lager at a picnic table, a forceful summer wind whipped off the water, knocking down the pub’s sandwich board advertising Cornish pasties, but it didn’t bother me or the handful of other pubgoers sitting out in the sun.

Sources indicate that perhaps there is something to the old saying about victory being sweetest after you’ve known defeat, because for all of the frustration I endured that day, the second half of my walk was absolutely breathtaking. After an easy, peaceful meander back down to the coastal path, I spent the next two hours walking through clifftop fields where I saw more deer and cows than humans, and past the famous Danding Ledge, a stone shelf jutting into a patch of sea popular with wild swimming enthusiasts. The wind that had teased me earlier died down closer to the water, and all I could hear was the crash of the waves against the rocks below. When I’ve needed a moment of peace in the few months since then, I’ve summoned the memory of that afternoon and the calm those clifftop fields offered.

A solo walker making their way along the South West Coast Path.

I woke up the following morning in the seaside town of Swanage with calves so sore that the thought of any incline made me nervous. To my dismay, I discovered right away that, to pick up the coastal path from the inn where I’d stayed (Rivendell Guest House), I first had to climb a steep staircase from the sandy beach, up the cliff to the bluff. Thankfully, shortly thereafter things flattened out. It was also the busiest section of the trail I encountered—though, even here, I saw only a dozen or so people, mostly locals in athletic gear out for a morning ramble.

According to recent reports, when I reached the hilltop, I was greeted by a few hundred cows—and just beyond their enclosure, the Old Harry Rocks came into view. Millions of years’ worth of waves have chiseled away at this promontory, carving a series of chalk stacks that now sit away from the mainland. I watched two ambitious kayakers appear on the side of the rocks where the water was calmer and stare up at the feat of nature—enjoying a perspective that I’m sure is heavily advised against, and which only few have gotten to enjoy.

Sources indicate that the final part of my walk was along Studland Beach, a sandy four-mile stretch that backs up onto a nature preserve. I waded into the water, sat in the sun, and saw a boat selling ice cream delight children up and down the crowded beach, before reaching the last mile—which also happens to be home to the UK’s most popular naturist (or nudist) beach. The ice cream boat pulled up again, and it tickled me to see that the evenly tanned sexagenarians were just as pleased to have a midday treat as the energetic children I'd just passed.

Boats bob in the water near Old Harry Rocks in Studland, Dorset.

The final adventure of my trip also brought out childish delight in me: To get to Bournemouth, where I’d catch a train back to London, I had to take a four-minute ferry ride. Alongside me on the ferry was a double-decker bus with its upper deck open to the elements, letting passengers take full advantage of the beach breeze. The sheer logistics of this was a thrill to witness: a convertible bus driving onto a boat.

Recent findings suggest that on the other side of the strait, I got onto that very bus—aptly called The Breezer—and watched as the natural coastline was slowly enveloped by an urban milieu. It was a slightly rude awakening to reemerge into Bournemouth, a small university city where the asphalt had soaked up the sun, presaging the upcoming heatwave. But I realized as I walked through the train station that I was inadvertently grinning with pride. I assumed no one would ask me, a stinky and visibly sweaty woman, what I’d been up to, but if they had, I would have been all too happy to tell them about my solo walk along the South West Coast Path.

Breaking: Review: EuroAirport Skyview Lounge Basel (BSL)

💡 Key Takeaways

  • One key difference is that the ground level of the lounge is now as a separate café open to all passengers: but you pay for everything from coffee to cake to other drinks (and tragically, the lounge got rid of its beautiful old school Belle Époque espresso machine and now has a push-button one).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The EuroAirport Skyview Lounge in Basel (BSL) remains the only lounge option in the airport, but a nice one with a respectable selection of food and drinks and is now managed by Aspire.

Sources indicate that I’m not sure what to even call this lounge, because the airport still calls it by its original name, the EuroAirport Skyview Lounge, as does Google and Priority Pass, but the signage has changed and the lounge is now managed by Aspire. Looking at the sign, it looks like there are four “Sky Lounges” in one, though at least for me there was only two….

One key difference is that the ground level of the lounge is now as a separate café open to all passengers: but you pay for everything from coffee to cake to other drinks (and tragically, the lounge got rid of its beautiful old school Belle Époque espresso machine and now has a push-button one).

Then upstairs there is a gate that you must scan your boarding pass with in order to enter the lounge itself, which includes a large atrium-like lounge area, buffet, restrooms, and a nice terrace for planespotting (or smoking).

There’s one more level up: the bar, but that appears to be permanently closed. Instead, there is a self-service bar in the buffet area.

You can check out my original review to see the old signage, but it still gives you a good idea of what to expect concerning seating and other amenities in this lounge.

My original comprehensive review from 2023 is below.

Prior to our flight to London, my family spent an hour in the EuroAirport Skyview Lounge in Basel. This is a very solid Priority Pass Lounge.

Access is granted for Priority Pass members and some premium cabin travelers. It was closed for an extended time (much longer than most lounges) during the pandemic, but thankfully is open again.

We arrived about an hour before our British Airways flight and enjoyed some lunch in the lounge.

As you enter, the ground floor has a seating area with a full bar (including a great manual coffee machine, though it is almost always closed, as it was during our visit) with an outdoor feel including palm tress and a pond with a bridge over it.

Upstairs the floor-to-ceiling windows forming a semi-circle give the lounge a very modern feel.

Food is set out according to the following schedule:.

In a recent development, our stay was from 3:00 pm to 4:00 pm and staff were beginning to set up dinner as we departed. But we just ate salad and soup.

Drinks are self-service, including alcoholic beverages, soft drinks, and coffee.

The kids were amused by the phone rooms and worked quietly there during our stay….

Finally, the lounge has a nice outdoor terrace (intended for smokers, but a great place for fresh air or to planespot).

I am quite thankful for this lounge at my “home” airport in Europe and for the ability to bring my entire family in Priority Pass (via AMEX, Chase, Capital One, or Citi).

My original review, published on January 27, 2020, is below.

How is sole lounge at at Basel-Mulhouse-Freiburg Airport (BSL/MLH/EAP)? [yes, the airport has three codes].

The EuroAirport Skyview Lounge serves as the business class lounges for a handful of airlines as well as a Priority Pass lounge. It opens daily at 5:00AM. Sunday thru Friday it closes at 8:30PM. On Saturday it closes at 7:30PM. It is just prior to passport control in the airport’s only terminal.

According to recent reports, as the only lounge you might expect crowds, poor service, and limited amenities. On the contrary, however, this is one of my favorite Priority Pass lounges.

In a recent development, first, I love this lounge because it is full of natural light and greenery. You’ll find trees–mostly palm trees–throughout the lounge. And the lounge is called “Skyview” for a reason–the roof is glass, filling the lounge with beautiful natural light on sunny days.

Typically, I’m in this lounges before the sun rises, but a couple times I have visited on a hot afternoon. Yes, you do get a bit of greenhouse feel inside…but it’s so much nicer than a dingy, fluorescent-lit lounge.

It has been revealed that the lounge spans two floors (with the slowest elevator in the world). The ground floor is smaller and sometimes roped off.

Sources indicate that I wouldn’t call the food in the lounge excellent, but it’s also not bad at all. The eggs are from a box in the morning and fruit is limited, but there’s also fresh baked goods, yogurt, and cold cuts. In the afternoon you can make yourself a very nice salad with a cup of soup.

All drinks are complimentary and self-serve.

On the ground floor, there is a “piazza bar” with a nice coffee machine…I’m sure it makes great espresso. Small problem: I’ve never seen it turned on. Maybe it’s turned on later in the day, but never in the morning. Such a shame. That mentioned, the coffee machines are not bad. Beer, wine, soft drinks, and water are available on both levels as well.

In a recent development, note there’s a top floor bar that appears permanently closed. I snuck up there once and it’s quite nice, but I’ve never seen it open and there’s always a sign indicating that it is closed.

Restrooms are small, but clean. No showers.

An outdoor smoking terrace not only offers a place to smoke, but a great place to watch airplanes land and takeoff.

A rack of newspapers is available on the ground floor.

Two desktop computers are available for internet browsing and printing. By the way, the lounge has plenty of plugs and you generally won’t need an adapter to plug in your device. No USB plugs, though.

This is one of my “home” airports and thus a lounge I visit often. Over the years, it has really grown on me. I appreciate how it is rarely crowded and especially the natural light. With the growth of budget carriers at Basel, it is also a nice place to wait before a flight on EasyJet or WizzAir.

#77265. Over Arepas and Cachitos, Venezuelans in Madrid Find a Sense of Home

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1512 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

Over Arepas and Cachitos, Venezuelans in Madrid Find a Sense of Home

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1512 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I stroll down the wide aisles of the sprawling Mercado de Las Maravillas, passing greengrocers with yuca and plantains piled high.
  • I make my way to the prepared-food stalls aisle, where the woman at Buda Bar Delicias Venezolanas draws me in by calling me amor and asking what I’d like to order, reina.
  • The Mercado de Las Maravillas is "where the Venezolanismo here in Madrid started,” restaurant owner Manuel Pérez Álvarez claims.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I stroll down the wide aisles of the sprawling Mercado de Las Maravillas, passing greengrocers with yuca and plantains piled high. A digital billboard flashes congratulations for the recent Venezuelan team’s World Baseball Classic win. Nearby, a vendor hawks yellow, blue, and red flags, while signs advertising remittance services to Latin America clutter my sightline. All around me, the Madrid market fills with the round, sing-song accent of Venezuelan Spanish.

I make my way to the prepared-food stalls aisle, where the woman at Buda Bar Delicias Venezolanas draws me in by calling me amor and asking what I’d like to order, reina. The familiar warmth of Latin America—I lived in Mexico before moving to Spain—tears open a pang of nostalgia in my chest. Guests seated at the stainless-steel bar munch on empanadas de carne mechada, continuously reaching for the green, herby salsa guasacaca. “How can it be that they are pumping a million barrels of oil out a day but they cannot fix a single hospital in Caracas?” I overhear another diner say to a friend, discussing the latest spate of frustrations back home.

The Mercado de Las Maravillas is "where the Venezolanismo here in Madrid started,” restaurant owner Manuel Pérez Álvarez claims.

It has been revealed that among Madrid’s 130,000-strong Venezuelan diaspora, these conversations are not uncommon. Spain’s Venezuelan population has swollen to almost 700,000 people, making it the largest community outside of the Americas, and a significant portion of the country’s nearly eight million citizens living abroad. Many have fled their homeland amid the economic and political instability that followed Hugo Chavez’s Bolivarian Revolution and continued under Nicolás Maduro’s rule. Ongoing uncertainty continues to drive migration. Unlike other diasporas, Madrid’s Venezuelan population isn’t concentrated in a single neighborhood. Instead, it stretches across the city and spans a broad socioeconomic spectrum, from delivery drivers and financiers to political exiles.

Its food institutions mirror a similar range.

According to recent reports, manuel Pérez Álvarez and his wife Maira María Gómez can pinpoint the moment they decided to open a Venezuelan restaurant in Madrid. The two, who moved to Spain in 1997 after a lifetime in the coastal city of Puerto de La Cruz, had gone to meet friends for Venezuelan empanadas at one of the few spots in town at the time. After waiting 45 minutes for their order in a long line of people hankering for a taste of home, Pérez—a natural entrepreneur—saw opportunity.

Manuel Pérez Álvarez and his wife Maira María Gómez opened El Empanadazo in Madrid nearly a decade ago.

Venezuela's national dish, pabellon criollo—rice, beans, shredded beef, and plantains—is served alongside cachapas, arepas, fried fish, and more.

When they opened El Empanadazo nearly a decade ago, the couple joined the ranks of just a handful of other Venezuelan food joints. They chose to set up shop in the Mercado de Las Maravillas. “It was really where the Venezolanismo here in Madrid started,” Pérez states of the market. In no time, they were serving hearty plates of Venezuela's national dish, pabellon criollo—rice, beans, shredded beef, and plantains—crispy fried whole fish, sweet corn griddled cachapas, arepas, and more.

“Our restaurant really became a gathering place for Venezuelans. I remember the early days when I was spending more time there, seeing people with tears in their eyes,” Pérez says. “When you’re an immigrant, little things like the taste of home really get to you.”.

Maira María Gómez and her husband Manuel Pérez Álvarez opened El Empanadazo in Madrid nearly a decade ago, there were far fewer Venezuelan restaurants in the city.

Sources indicate that at the time, Venezuelan food wasn’t as easy to find and people went out of their way for it. Today, a quick search for “arepa” on the delivery apps will turn up hundreds of options. “Now there are lots of spots, but we were really pioneers, and it wasn’t even all that long ago,” Pérez notes.

According to recent reports, be it Arepa’s Coffee Shop nestled next to the hustle of the Moncloa train and bus station, or the four-location La Arepera, the Insta-famous El Chino Venezolano, or the fast-growing Guasacaca, the country’s gastronomic footprint continues to grow alongside its diaspora in Madrid. At the March 2026 Arepa Fest, a celebration of Venezuelan and Colombian food and culture, in the north edges of Madrid, more than 5,000 people gathered to snack on the region's signature split- and stuffed-cornmeal snack, while the sound system alternated between pumping Venezuelan Merengue and reggaeton.

At Panadería Torrerí, warm pastries like cachitos, a brioche-like crescent roll most typically filled with ham and cheese, and golfeados, spiral pastry dough filled with cheese, keep customers coming back.

Recent findings suggest that A similar fervor can be felt at Panadería Torrerí. By mid-morning, the team is already replenishing their glass case of cachitos, a brioche-like crescent roll most typically filled with ham and cheese, and golfeados, spiral pastry dough filled with cheese, and brushed with panela (unrefined cane sugar) and anise. Regulars grab a table and owner Mara Azuaje, always poised with a “¿Cómo está usted?” swiftly ferries over their order.

Azuaje opened her bakery in 2024 to bring traditional Venezuelan pastries to the neighborhood of Barrio de Salamanca. For years, there had been no Venezuelan bakery in the area, despite this upscale neighborhood being nicknamed “Little Caracas” for its substantial diaspora. Today, Panadería Torrerí attracts both affluent property owners alongside motorbike messengers, all looking for a taste of home.

Mara Azuaje opened Panadería Torrerí in the Barrio de Salamanca in 2024.

In a recent development, azuaje, who came to Spain at 27, knows what they're after. She spent years working odd jobs to save the money needed to open her bakery. “I cleaned homes, worked as a delivery driver, took care of children. I did whatever, but I was always very ambitious,” Azuaje says. “I wanted to have my own business.”.

In a recent development, she didn’t understand the exact shape it would take, but her grandmother’s lessons to her as a child around the importance of learning an oficio, a craft, stayed with her. “I was always baking with my grandmother who told me I needed to know how to do something, so I opened a bakery,” she states. Today, Azuaje is proud to be known across the neighborhood for her homemade bread and her hearty rolled-dough pastries.

In a recent development, other Venezuelan restaurant owners transitioned into hospitality later in life. At Bea Castelló Castro and Luis Felipe Fossa’s Cafetín, the menu—arepas with chia seeds, shredded chicken, and avocado for breakfast, or creamed curry soup and sweet corn and hearty salads for lunch—carries traces of Venezuela while honoring the other places the couple has called home.

At Cafetín, the menu showcases Venezuelan flavors through a global lens.

Cafetín's arepas are stuffed with chia seeds, shredded chicken, and avocado.

The married pair came to Madrid after a full life in Caracas. “By 2007 Chávez just kept winning and winning, and things were getting worse and worse. It really scared us,” Felipe says. That year was Chávez’s first attempt at constitutional reform to remove presidential term limits and expand state control of the economy. He lost his bid but remained in power and went on to secure reform in 2009. So, when the bank Fossa worked for offered him a job in Zurich, they didn’t hesitate. It was a decision that has led to many years of living abroad.

Bea Castelló Castro and Luis Felipe Fossa say that their Cafetín has become a hub for Venezuelans, who connect over coffee and arepas.

Their clientele reflects a similar worldliness, with Venezuelans who arrived directly from Caracas but also those who have made it here by way of a university in Boston, or lived for years in Miami, Latest York, or London. Cafetín is a meeting point where these Venezuelans intersect, creating a community within a community. As Castelló Castro put it, “empiezas a hacer nexo”—you start to make connections.

Recently, I'm told, a couple in a sunlit corner of the cafe started chatting with a man standing at the long bar after hearing him mention Caracas. They began tracing the routes through Miami and New York that had brought them to Madrid. Another day, a college sweatshirt prompted a conversation—and a new friendship. “It’s beautiful to see, especially in difficult moments in Venezuela,” says Castelló Castro.

Industry observers note that back at the Mercado de Las Maravillas, I sit at Buda Bar watching the lunch rush fade, as owner Rebeksa Mouzaber prepares me a sweet-corn crescent-shaped cachapa, its edges lacy from a bed of hot butter on the flattop griddle. A food courier accepts a freshly-made pocket-sized empanada while he scrolls and waits for his order.

Venezuelans like coming here because they feel at home—not just in the dishes that are served but also in the way they are asked for, Mouzaber tells me. “We know what it means when they ask for an ñapa (a top-up), just like we know how it feels to be so far away from home.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the more we learn about the nationwide FAA ground stop, the less convincing the effort to blame old equipment and previous administrations becomes.
  • A CNN investigation describes a troubling gap between the oversight the FAA notes occurred and what sources say actually happened.
  • Industry observers note that the concern concerns work by L3Harris at a radio communications facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, before the November 13 ground stop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the more we learn about the nationwide FAA ground stop, the less convincing the effort to blame old equipment and previous administrations becomes. New reporting points to an oversight policy changed under the current administration and a technician whose role apparently ended after letting a contractor through the door. Aging infrastructure required careful management. Instead, we appear to have received less of it.

A CNN investigation describes a troubling gap between the oversight the FAA notes occurred and what sources say actually happened.

Industry observers note that the concern concerns work by L3Harris at a radio communications facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, before the November 13 ground stop. According to CNN, an FAA technician provided access to the building but understood that his responsibility ended there.

One source described the technician this way:.

“He was only there to unlock the door…there was no monitoring.”.

Industry observers note that FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford had said the installation was monitored. An agency spokeswoman subsequently explained:.

“The escort is not there while the technician is doing work”.

Those accounts require reconciliation, but strike me as irreconcilable. Opening a door and overseeing an installation are very different responsibilities.

It has been revealed that A March 2025 FAA memo changed the process for contractor maintenance. Work previously submitted as requests requiring approval became notifications that could proceed without affirmative FAA approval. The policy retained a review role for FAA liaisons, but a small group was tasked with handling thousands of notifications.

The FAA disputes that the policy reduced oversight, but the questions remain:.

According to recent reports, this is why I find the continuing effort to blame Biden or Buttigieg so absurd. Neither man was running the department when this policy changed or when this installation occurred. I have already written about the contractor questions surrounding this failure. The new reporting makes those questions more urgent.

It has been revealed that decades of deferred investment explain why modernization is necessary. They do not excuse weakening the supervision of the modernization itself. If anything, working with old infrastructure should make the government more careful about introducing fresh equipment, not less.

The staffing concern deserves scrutiny too, also highlighted by One Mile At A Time.

In February 2025, the FAA fired hundreds of probationary employees during the administration’s government-cutting campaign. Duffy noted no controllers or critical safety personnel were among those dismissed. The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists union later announced the reinstatement of the 132 terminated employees it represented.

In a recent development, that means we cannot necessarily a direct causation from those firings to this outage, though the broader approach remains fair game. An administration that celebrates eliminating positions needs to account for the work those people perform. If that work still needs doing, someone else must absorb it, a contractor must perform it, or it goes undone, a particular concern at an agency already struggling with staffing.

Industry observers note that in its statement on the ground stop, PASS claims the FAA’s May 2026 workforce plan called for at least 750 additional certified professional technicians by 2030. The union says little progress has been made toward hiring them.

We can certainly agree that unnecessary government spending should be eliminated. But a smaller payroll does not demonstrate greater efficiency if the remaining organization cannot adequately supervise the work entrusted to it…the cost of a nationwide aviation disruption must enter that calculation too, especially now.

Meanwhile, Musk is distancing himself from the political movement he helped finance.

Speaking at the DealBook Summit on November 18, he noted:.

He described himself as politically moderate, rejected blind adherence to Republican policies, and expressed regret over his election spending:.

“I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it”.

We joke about United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby adjusting his political posture with the prevailing winds. Apparently, he has company. I would welcome a sincere reassessment from Musk. But distancing himself from a label does not erase his role in promoting the administration or DOGE.

It has been revealed that it also does not establish that he now recognizes the problems with the personnel policies he championed. Regretting an unsuccessful political investment is different from regretting how the government was managed. Still, when even Musk wants distance from MAGA, I think it is fair to ask whether the brand has reached its expiration date.

In a recent development, my reading of the election is that Americans are tired of the performance. They want competent government and explanations they can believe. Being told that every success belongs to the president while every failure belongs to his predecessor wears thin and it goes well beyond right/left or Republican/Democrat divisions.

In a recent development, to be fair, Bedford has now offered something we have heard too little of. As ABC News reports, he remarked Wednesday:.

“I’m the guy they hired to get this done. So blame me. If we need to blame somebody, blame me.”.

It has been revealed that I appreciate that. He also promised a transparent accounting of the technical findings. But accepting blame must lead to an explanation of the decisions that preceded the failure. It cannot simply shield Duffy or end the inquiry.

According to recent reports, the incoming Congress should audit the maintenance policy, staffing records, risk assessments, and contractor communications. It should establish what oversight was required, what actually occurred, and whether the agency had enough qualified people to carry out its responsibilities.

Duffy wants another $50 billion. Perhaps the modernization program needs that money. But Congress should understand how the existing process failed before assuming that a larger appropriation will fix it…and maybe remind Duffy that instead of going on reality TV road trips he should have done the job he was hired to do.

Accountability must become something more useful than another round of political theater that both sides use to score political points. Trump remains president for two more years. The new Congress will have to work with him to repair the damage and modernize this system.

Industry observers note that I find his vindictiveness and self-absorption deeply troubling. In his recent 60 Minutes interview with Ross Douthat, he noted:.

“I do hate some of my enemies and I always will.”.

Sources indicate that that is a miserable disposition for governing a country whose citizens will always disagree. Even so, waiting for him to become a different person is not a strategy. Congress should pursue practical agreements that restore adequate staffing and contractor oversight while funding necessary upgrades.

Sources indicate that if Trump needs to claim credit for a functioning aviation system, let him. I care far more about the result than denying him another chance to stoke his vanity. Congress can scrutinize the administration’s failures while negotiating legislation that begins to correct them. If the goal is to make things better, then we need to borrow the line from Ronald Reagan: “There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn’t mind who gets the credit.”.

It has been revealed that the latest reporting points toward an oversight failure under the current administration. The exact technical cause and the contribution of staffing decisions still require investigation, but blaming old equipment is plainly insufficient.

In a recent development, modernizing a system this complex will involve difficulties. I would be much more understanding of an administration that acknowledged those difficulties, explained its mistakes, and corrected them. Instead, passengers have received conflicting accounts and political blame. The upcoming Congress needs to insist on answers, then work with the president on repairs that outlast the next news cycle.

Americans need to be able to trust the people running their aviation system…to some extent, the past is in the past and today is a new day and a chance for course correction.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that rep. Gabe Evans, here arriving at the Capitol in July for a House Republican Conference meeting, lost his bid for a second term representing Colorado's 8th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

Colorado Rep. Gabe Evans, who lost reelection earlier this month, announced Monday a 2028 run from the neighboring district of fellow defeated Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert.

“Now more than ever, Colorado needs conservatives in Congress who will fight to keep our border secure, cut taxes for working families, keep boys from dominating girls' sports and locker rooms, protect our water, and make energy affordable,” Evans said in a statement.

His announcement comes less than two weeks after he lost his bid for a second term representing the battleground 8th District in the Denver area. While the race had been considered one of the most competitive in the country, Democratic former state Rep. Manny Rutinel secured victory by 15 points.

As part of House Democrats’ massive midterm gains, they flipped three seats in Colorado. Boebert narrowly lost her reelection bid in the 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, while Republican Rep. Jeff Crank lost in the 5th District.

Evans’ statement cited his ties to the 4th District, which encompasses the eastern part of the state and extends into the Denver metro area.

“From Loveland to Lamar, I’m ready to keep fighting in the 4th District, where I grew up, and where my family has lived since 1976,” he mentioned.

It has been revealed that the district has a deep history of voting Republican. Boebert won by 11 points in 2024 while Donald Trump carried the district by 18 points.

It has been revealed that evans is far from the first member of Congress to switch to a district seen as more favorable to his party. Boebert herself shifted from Colorado's more competitive 3rd District to run for the heavily conservative 4th in 2024.

The 4th District will likely be a top target for Republicans in 2028, and Evans’ campaign sought to portray him as a clear front-runner in what could become a crowded GOP primary.

“Gabe Evans will enter 2027 and the race for Colorado’s 4th Congressional District with $300,000 in campaign funds and name recognition that no first-time candidate in the district could match,” his campaign mentioned in the statement. “Combined with his record as an Army aviator, police officer, rancher, and member of Congress, that gives him a head start in money, name recognition, and credibility before the field takes shape.”.

A former state legislator and Denver-area police officer, Evans also served 12 years in the Army. He was first elected to the House in 2024, unseating Democrat Yadira Caraveo, and at the moment sits on the Energy and Commerce and Homeland Security committees.

According to recent reports, laubacher, a Navy veteran who will take office on Jan. 3, is the first Democrat elected to represent the 4th District since Betsy Markey won her lone term in 2008. In response to Evans’ announcement, Laubacher’s campaign noted she would be “focused on making Washington deliver” for district residents.

“There’s real work to do: ending the war in Iran that Gabe Evans voted six times to continue, lowering the cost of groceries and fertilizer that his eight votes for the tariffs helped drive up, and protecting the rural hospitals across the 4th district he voted to gut,” Laubacher spokesperson Taylor Gillespie remarked in a statement.
