I suspect these planes will primarily be used for service to North America, or possibly for service from secondary cities in Brazil to Europe. Officially, for now the airline just claims these planes will be used to “strengthen connectivity between South America and more distant destinations.”.

    Earlier this year, LATAM’s CEO did drop some hints that the plane could fly from Lima (LIM) and Brasilia (BSB) to the United States, and from Fortaleza (FOR) to Europe, though no final decisions have been unveiled.

    It has been revealed that we can expect LATAM to offer an all-upcoming passenger experience (by the carrier’s standards) onboard the Airbus A321XLRs. The airline plans to configure the planes with a total of 174 seats, including:.

    It has been revealed that throughout the plane, passengers can expect the Panasonic Astrova entertainment system, with over 2,300 hours of content, including 330 movies and 1,200 TV shows. Bluetooth audio will also be available at all seats, so that passengers can connect to their own headphones. The A321XLR will also be equipped with SES Wi-Fi, with LATAM Pass members getting complimentary browsing or messaging, depending on their membership tier and ticket type.

    LATAM’s A321XLR business class will feature the Thompson Aero VantageSOLO product. So there will be 12 herringbone seats in a 1-1 configuration, with seats spread across six rows. This means all seats will have direct aisle access and doors. Business class seats will feature 19″ 4K OLED screens, AC power outlets, USB-C charging, and wireless charging.

    Sources indicate that it also looks like the front row seats will be pretty special, as they’ll feature quite a bit of extra space, including a closet and wardrobe. It remains to be seen how the airline will monetize that extra space, if at all (maybe they’ll just be reserved for certain types of passengers?).

    LATAM’s A321XLR business class will feature the Recaro R3 product. So there will be 162 seats in a 3-3 configuration, with six rows having extra legroom, and 21 rows having standard legroom. Economy class seats will feature 13″ 4K OLED screens, as well as USB-C outlets.

    According to recent reports, the A321XLR is impressive for its range, and it’s understandable that the economics of such a small plane for long haul flying can be challenging. As a result, we’re really seeing airlines try to maximize capacity as much as possible, and this is also leading to so many airlines having very similar premium products on planes.

    LATAM will have herringbone seats on the A321XLR, just like… well, all current operators that use this primarily as a long haul aircraft, with the exception of Aer Lingus.

    For those keeping track at home, the Thompson Aero VantageSOLO product is what you’ll find in JetBlue’s Mint business class on select A321neo/LR aircraft, and it’s also what you’ll find in Iberia’s A321XLR business class.

    While American’s A321XLR business class looks similar, it’s based on the Collins Aerospace Aurora seating platform, and that’s also what Air Canada has selected. Meanwhile United’s A321XLR business class also looks similar, but is based on the Elevate Altitude platform.

    Admittedly these planes all have better business class products than we found on long haul Boeing 757s years ago (the most direct replacement), and the tech is also greatly updated. That being said, as a passenger experience geek, this sure is a boring plane… “you get a herringbone seat, you get a herringbone seat, you get a herringbone seat, everyone gets a herringbone seat!”.

    While not quite A321XLRs, credit to ITA Airways’ A321neo business class and Etihad’s A321LR business class for having reverse herringbone seats.

    To LATAM’s credit, I will say that the cabin finishes look gorgeous, so I hope they look as nice in real life as they do in renderings.

    Recent findings suggest that in early 2027, LATAM expects to start taking delivery of the Airbus A321XLR, which the airline aims to use to grow into fresh markets. The airline has now revealed what we can expect onboard these planes, and it includes herringbone seats with direct aisle access and doors in business class.

    Ultimately the cabin looks sleek, and it’s cool to see this in South America, where no other airline is at the moment offering such an experience. But still, it’s hard to get too excited when so many airlines are introducing a similar product.

    LATAM in general deserves credit for the extent to which it’s elevating the passenger experience in Latin America, as we’ve seen the airline introduce two latest wide body business class products over the past several years.

    When Rep.-elect Chris Rabb first worked on Capitol Hill in the 1990s, it didn’t exactly inspire him to want to go into politics.

    Working for Carol Moseley Braun, the first Black woman elected as a U.S. senator, Rabb saw threats and “just vile things” directed at her.

    “My entrée to service behind the scenes was seeing voluminous amounts of violence, hate speech and death threats against my boss, and I thought to myself, ‘Why would anyone want to serve?’” he mentioned.

Dwight Evans in a deep-blue district based in West Philadelphia.

    Rabb is one of more than a dozen incoming members who have worked on the Hill before, ranging from interns to chiefs of staff and everything in between.

    Unlike some in the 100-plus-strong freshman class, they already know their way around the hallways. And Rabb has some advice for his new colleagues: “Treat your staff well. Take care of your staff; they’ll take care of you.”.

    Here are some of the former staffers who will join the House in January.

    Before his time on the D.C. Council, he worked as her legislative counsel, watching her navigate a role with limited power in her perennial fight for statehood.

    “I need to make sure I’m developing a national profile for this seat,” he said, vowing to continue the quest for full representation even as President Donald Trump seeks to exert more control over the District.

Rick Scott, R-Fla., and plans to keep pushing for a bill he helped draft that aims to crack down on foreign surrogacy contracts. “We are currently selling American children to China, our No. 1 adversary,” Rogers said, describing it as “deplorable.”.

    Rogers will succeed retiring GOP Rep. Neal Dunn in the Florida Panhandle.

    He faced a rare formal disapproval vote in the House over the move. But García has insisted she is more than a hand-picked successor, saying on her campaign website that she has “delivered solutions rooted in lived experience.”.

    The son of Ghanaian immigrants, Boafo is a state delegate who has lobbied on the Hill for tech firm Oracle.

    It has been revealed that he also worked as campaign manager for Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, earning an endorsement from the retiring longtime Democrat and campaign cash from groups aligned with him.

    Boafo prevailed in a crowded primary, even as Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi threw her weight behind a different candidate, former Capitol Police officer Harry Dunn.

    Sell worked under then-House Agriculture Chair Larry Combest during the 2000 crop insurance overhaul and the fight over the 2002 farm bill. He later joined his former boss in launching an agricultural lobbying firm, Combest, Sell and Associates.

    “I feel supremely fortunate to have wandered into Jerry Nadler’s political orbit as a teenager 30 years ago, and then to have worked in his congressional office a decade later,” Lasher wrote in an opinion piece for City & State Upcoming York.

    Backed by the retiring Nadler, the self-described “nerd” beat out a couple of big names in the primary, including a Kennedy family heir. Another former boss endorsed him, too: Gov. Kathy Hochul. Before serving as a New York state assemblyman, Lasher worked as her policy director.

    In a recent development, villegas ousted GOP Rep. David Valadao in a closely watched race in the San Joaquin Valley.

    In a recent development, A San Diego City councilmember, Von Wilpert flipped the seat held by Republican Rep. Darrell Issa, who decided not to run for reelection under a map redrawn by Democrats.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Industry observers note that brian T.

    It has been revealed that ‘E verything’s Up to Date in Kansas City” — that few minutes of pure effervescence in Oklahoma refers to Kansas City circa 1907, when it was in the middle of its version of the City Beautiful movement. New boulevards, new, fancy neighborhoods, hundreds of fountains, and much more were in the works. The sparkle of a new art museum was in the civic eye, too. The Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art didn’t open its doors until 1933, but better late than never. It’s an essential visit for art lovers.

    Industry observers note that I visited last month and saw the very enjoyable exhibition American Prospects and Landscape Photography, 1839 to Today. It presents Joel Sternfeld’s lovely, often sad, wry, late-1970s and early-1980s landscape photographs in the context of the American landscape-photography genre. I love Sternfeld’s work. Born in 1944, he was the cutting-edge photographer who took color landscape photography mainstream, mostly through American Prospects, his portfolio of photographs published in book form in 1987. Color? Cutting-edge in the ’80s? Well, 1987 is about to be 40 years ago, so it qualifies as days of yore, and what has became American Prospects started in the late ’70s, when Sternfeld started an epic road trip to make art about Americans and the land. Landscape photography was, à la Ansel Adams, commonly in black and white, thought to evoke grandeur and mystery. What pushed Sternfeld to color was the advent of Kodak Vericolor III film in the 1970s. It delivered accurate, vibrant color and was good for various lighting and especially skin tones.

    Industry observers note that brian T. Allen is National Review’s art critic.

    On “Wry and Wistful Landscapes at Kansas City’s Splendid Nelson-Atkins Museum”.

    #77207. Lufthansa Ordered The Airbus A350-1000 In 2023 & Got It Before The Boeing 777-9 It Ordered In 2013

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1472 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Lufthansa Ordered The Airbus A350-1000 In 2023 & Got It Before The Boeing 777-9 It Ordered In 2013

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1472 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that lufthansa is set to be the launch customer for the upcoming Boeing 777-9.
    • Recent findings suggest that in 2023, Lufthansa ordered the Airbus A350-1000.
    • Sources indicate that lufthansa first ordered the 777-9 in 2013, initially placing 34 orders for the aircraft.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that lufthansa is set to be the launch customer for the upcoming Boeing 777-9. The problem, however, is that it was scheduled to enter service in 2020. The entry-into-service date for the 777-9 has been pushed back several times, and the aircraft has become one of the most delayed projects in commercial aviation history. What's more, the 777-9 is not a newly introduced aircraft; rather, it's an overhaul of an existing aircraft type (albeit an extremely thorough one). The 777-9's EIS is now set for 2027.

    Recent findings suggest that in 2023, Lufthansa ordered the Airbus A350-1000. While the A350-1000 competes with the 777-9, Lufthansa will operate both in complementary roles. Strikingly, Lufthansa has already received its first A350-1000, with the first example having been delivered in November 2026. The German flag carrier ordered the A350-1000 a full ten years after it first placed its orders for the 777-9, yet its first A350-1000 has arrived a few months before the first 777-9 is set to be delivered, and this assumes that the current 2027 timeline will stick.

    Sources indicate that lufthansa first ordered the 777-9 in 2013, initially placing 34 orders for the aircraft. Interestingly, this was the first time the airline had ordered a passenger variant of the 777, and it will be the first to operate the type once it's ready. In 2019, Lufthansa converted 14 of its firm orders to options, leaving it with 20 firm orders and 24 options for the 777-9. In addition, Lufthansa Group also holds orders for seven 777-8Fs to be operated by Lufthansa Cargo, and it will be the first European operator of the aircraft.

    The group ordered ten A350-1000s in 2023, as part of a larger order that included five A350-900s and seven Boeing 787s. The A350-1000 order was later increased to 15 units, and they will mainly operate out of Munich. Lufthansa took its first A350-1000 in November 2026, and including subsequent A350-900 orders, the airline group has ordered 75 A350s in total, split between 60 A350-900s and 15 A350-1000s.

    While the A350-1000 will primarily be a Munich aircraft, the 777-9 is mainly intended to operate out of Frankfurt, and it will initially replace the airline's Boeing 747-400 fleet. While the configuration has not been officially revealed, the 747-400s that will be replaced by the 777-9s feature a relatively dense configuration with no first class cabin. As such, some of the airline's 777-9s may have only a three-class interior, while others may be delivered with a four-class layout and first class.

    Industry observers note that despite being in development for nearly 14 years, the 777-9 is still not certified. The program has repeatedly encountered setbacks, and there have been multiple delays to the aircraft's certification. Boeing hoped to start delivering the 777-9 in 2020, but now anticipates that the aircraft will begin being delivered to customers in 2027. Lufthansa, meanwhile, has removed the 777-9 from internal planning for the 2027 summer schedule, meaning that it does not expect to have received a significant number of 777-9s, if any at all, before the season ends.

    The aircraft's certification was heavily impacted by the two fatal Boeing 737 MAX 8 crashes in 2018 and 2019, which led to a 20-month grounding of the 737 MAX worldwide. Boeing faced increased scrutiny from the FAA following the tragic crashes, including closer oversight of the 777-9 certification program. COVID stretched out the timeline again, and multiple engineering and design challenges have further delayed the aircraft's certification.

    Industry observers note that the 777-9 features several newly introduced design elements that make it quite different from earlier 777 models. This includes a new carbon-composite wing, new engines, a fuselage stretch, a thoroughly updated cabin, and more. This means there are more variables with the 777-9 than with a project like the Airbus A320neo, where almost everything was identical to its predecessors apart from the engines.

    According to recent reports, most recently, the FAA shifted resources towards certifying the 737 MAX 7 and 737 MAX 10, which are now ready to fly. With the two upcoming 737 variants approved to enter service when ready, the FAA can allocate more resources to the 777-9 program. In addition, General Electric is awaiting FAA approval on a new mid-seal design for the GE9X, while certification flights are still ongoing.

    Recent findings suggest that unlike most customers for the aircraft, Lufthansa doesn't plan to use the 777-9 as its flagship aircraft. Instead, the 747-8 will remain in this role, with Lufthansa operating 17 examples out of its Frankfurt hub, all of which will receive fresh interiors. The 20 777-9s will slot underneath the 747-8s. In Frankfurt, Lufthansa is also operating the 787-9, which will serve as its smallest widebody to operate thinner routes, along with some A350-900s. Meanwhile, the airline will operate most A350-900s out of Munich, alongside the A350-1000 and the Airbus A380.

    The airline is currently flying just three Airbus A330-300s, which are set to be transferred to other airlines within Lufthansa Group by the end of the year. In addition, there are still six 747-400s flying and 11 A340-300s, which are meant to be fully retired by 2028 as the carrier takes more 777-9s and 787-9s. Furthermore, Lufthansa is operating eight A380s, which are receiving latest business class seats that are different from the new Allegris interiors, and they should remain in service until the 2030s.

    Lufthansa Current Widebody Fleet (Planespotters.net).

    Sources indicate that looking ahead, Lufthansa's fleet will center on the A350-900 family and the 787-9, with the A350-900s mainly concentrated in Munich and the 787s based in Frankfurt. The 777-9s and 747-8s will remain Lufthansa's larger options for routes out of Frankfurt, while the equivalent for Munich will be the A350-1000 and A380-800. The A380s should be the next aircraft type to go in the 2030s, while the 747-8 is expected to remain in the fleet long-term.

    It has been revealed that while the seat count by cabin has yet to be revealed, the 777-9s will feature Lufthansa's Allegris interiors. The 777-9 was originally meant to launch the Allegris seats in 2020, but delays with the program led Lufthansa to introduce the seats on the A350-900 four years after their intended launch. For the most part, the Allegris cabins are the same for different aircraft from a customer experience standpoint (although different suppliers manufacture the seats for different aircraft).

    In a recent development, the new first class cabins feature one row with three suites across, while the suites themselves offer near-ceiling-height partitions and sliding doors, along with modernized technology and in-suite climate controls. Uniquely, the center suite is sized to accommodate two passengers traveling together as a couple, with two seats side by side, a larger monitor, and double-bed capability. In a sense, it's one suite that can accommodate two passengers, which is a very unusual proposition.

    Recent findings suggest that the Allegris business class seats offer direct aisle access, alternating between a three-abreast and a four-abreast layout. The seats are in a staggered layout, with some being angled toward the aisle in a manner that closely resembles United Airlines' last-generation Polaris seats. Lufthansa offers five different types of seats in the Allegris business class cabin, which each offer progressively more space and privacy for a fee. In addition, Allegris includes fresh seats for premium economy and economy.

    The A350-1000 and 777-9 are competitors in the sense that they're the largest aircraft sold by Airbus and Boeing. But while airlines do compare them, they have significant differences, the most obvious being size. The 777-9 is much larger than the A350-1000 or the 777-300ER, and it can carry nearly as many passengers as the 747-400. The A350-1000 has lower trip costs and greater range, but the 777-9 has lower seat-mile costs and greater cargo volume.

    Because these aircraft are quite compelling in different ways, several airlines have elected to buy both rather than choose. The A350-1000 can serve as a large ultra-long-range aircraft, while the 777-9 is typically bought for its floor space to serve as a flagship aircraft. Lufthansa has installed a first class cabin on its A350-1000s, but it's actually the exception, and Lufthansa has one of the largest first class fleets in the world.

    Sources indicate that the carrier's new A350-1000s can carry 300 passengers, and while the layout for the 777-9 has not been revealed, it's believed these planes will likely seat over 350 passengers. In addition, the airline plans to base the two at different hubs. Overall, they serve different purposes for Lufthansa and multiple other airlines.     Industry News: Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited Card Review: Is The $295 Fee Worth It?

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Graphite™ Business Cash Unlimited Card introduced in March 2026.
    • Sources indicate that however, there are some things that could make this card worthwhile, including a potentially lucrative welcome offer, a solid return on spending, and some credits that can help offset the annual fee.
    • This post is my in-depth Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited review.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Graphite™ Business Cash Unlimited Card introduced in March 2026. On the surface, the card sounds rather uncompetitive — it has a $295 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and offers “just” 2% cash back on everyday spending, with limited bonus categories.

    Sources indicate that however, there are some things that could make this card worthwhile, including a potentially lucrative welcome offer, a solid return on spending, and some credits that can help offset the annual fee. If your business spends a lot, you value having an Amex, and you just want to earn simple cash back without a complex rewards structure, this could be a good option.

    This post is my in-depth Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited review. Is the card worth it, and if so, under what circumstances? And what are the best alternatives?

    Link: Learn more about the Graphite™ Business Cash Unlimited Card.

    Before I get into my Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited review, let me briefly summarize the key details of the card:.

    Beyond that, here are what I consider to be some of the major pros and cons of the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited:.

    With the above out of the way, let’s look at the various aspects of the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited, from the welcome offer, to the fees, to the rewards structure, to the other perks. This card is fairly straightforward, so there’s not all that much to understand, for better or worse.

    It has been revealed that the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited presently has a welcome offer where you can earn as high as $2,000 cash back after spending $50,000 within the first six months on eligible purchases. Reward Dollars can be redeemed as statement credits to offset transactions, or as a payment method for Amazon purchases.

    Given that the card ordinarily offers at least 2% cash back, that means spending $50,000 could earn you a minimum of $3,000 (if offered the full bonus amount), equivalent to 6% cash back on that amount of spending, which is solid.

    In a recent development, admittedly the spending requirement is massive (it averages out to $8,333 per month over the course of six months), but I do think businesses that spend a lot might find this to be achievable. Furthermore, it’s nice that you have six months to complete the spending requirement, while many other cards give you only three months to reach the spending requirement.

    If you’re applying for the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited, be aware of Amex’s general restrictions on applying for cards, including the “once in a lifetime rule.” That means you’re not eligible for the welcome offer on the card if you’ve already had this card, though you are potentially eligible for the bonus if you’ve had other Amex cards.

    According to recent reports, anecdotally, I find Amex business cards to be quite easy to get approved for. I also love how with Amex, you can know if you’ll be approved with no credit score impact — the hard pull only happens after you’re told if you’re approved, and you accept the offer.

    Also keep in mind that if you’re concerned about staying under Chase’s 5/24 limit, applying for an Amex business card won’t count toward that, since it doesn’t show up on your personal credit report in that way.

    Sources indicate that when it comes to credit score, there’s not a consistent credit score you need to get approved for the card, as it’s one of only many factors that determines eligibility. Personally, I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected.

    The Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited has an annual fee of $295 (Rates & Fees), which is definitely on the steep side, especially given the relatively narrow appeal of the credits offered on the card, which require a lot of spending.

    With the card’s 2% cash back rewards structure, you’d essentially recoup the annual fee (in terms of rewards) after $14,750 in spending.

    Industry observers note that the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited has an authorized user fee of $95 for the first 5 cards, and a $95 annual fee for each thereafter (Rates & Fees), though you can also get a no annual fee Employee Business Expense Card with no additional fee. Still, that’s a rather steep authorized user fee for a card that doesn’t actually offer many incremental perks. You can add up to 99 employee cards to your account.

    Sources indicate that the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited has no preset spending limit. The idea is that this gives you flexibility in ways that traditional credit cards don’t. The amount you can spend adapts based on factors such as your purchase, payment, and credit history. Rather than having a set limit, you could grow your purchasing power the more you consistently use your card and regularly make payments.

    According to recent reports, in fairness, it is also worth mentioning that not having a preset spending limit can also lead to some declines if the amount you can charge decreases, so it’s a little less predictable than a regular credit card. However, I find that more often than not, it works in the favor of cardmembers.

    No Preset Spending Limit means your spending limit is flexible. Unlike a traditional card with a set limit, the amount you can spend adapts based on factors such as your purchase, payment, and credit history.

    In terms of its rewards structure, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited offers 2% cash back on eligible purchases. On top of that, the card offers 5% cash back on flights and prepaid hotels booked through American Express Travel® Online. Just to do some very basic math:.

    Industry observers note that all cash back on the card is earned as Reward Dollars, which can be redeemed as statement credits to offset transactions, or as a payment method for Amazon purchases. Unfortunately there are no other redemption options, so you couldn’t directly deposit the cash back into a business checking account, or anything like that.

    2% cash back on credit card spending is the “gold standard,” as I see it, so that’s excellent, and what everyone should be aiming for, at a minimum.

    Recent findings suggest that meanwhile the 5% cash back on Amex Travel might sound appealing, but there are some catches. If you can route travel spending that way, it’s a good option, but the catch is that you may sometimes find lower rates elsewhere, so there could be an opportunity cost to booking that way.

    The Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited offers up to $2,400 in American Express One AP® statement credits, after spending $250,000 on eligible purchases on the card in a calendar year. Statement credits will be applied to the monthly bill charged to the card for Amex’s accounts payable solution, One AP, for the following calendar year, and this includes an auto-renewing platform access fee.

    American Express One AP® is an accounts payable solution that can help transform the way your business pays suppliers. With One AP, you can streamline your supplier invoice payments on a single platform and pay by virtual card, check, and ACH. Enrollment is required.

    According to recent reports, this program charges a $200 monthly fee to pay vendors with non-cards, plus has a fee for checks and ACHs over a certain limit. So the $2,400 annual credit can potentially fully cover your monthly fee. While this is potentially a nice feature, keep in mind that many platforms already offer this as a built in feature at no extra cost, so it’s not really that special.

    Industry observers note that the Amex Graphite Business Cash Unlimited offers the Pay Over Time feature, whereby cardmembers can carry a balance with interest on eligible charges, up to the Pay Over Time limit. The way this works, eligible charges will automatically be added to a Pay Over Time balance, up to the Pay Over Time limit.

    You can choose to pay for these charges over time with interest, or you can pay your full balance each month, whichever is best for your business. You must pay in full any charge or a portion of a charge that is not added to a Pay Over Time balance.

    Personally, I recommend paying the balance in full each billing cycle if possible, to avoid interest charges, especially given how high they can be. However, I think it’s worth clarifying that the Pay Over Time option is possible, given that this isn’t a traditional credit card.

    Recent findings suggest that it’s also worth emphasizing the difference between the Pay Over Time and the Pay In Full Limit. The latter could be an amount that has to be paid in full, and there’s no option to pay that over time with interest charges.

    The Amex Graphite Business Cash Card earns 2% cash back, and I consider that to be the minimum “gold standard” of credit card rewards. So the card’s rewards structure is perfectly fine. The 5% cash back on travel is also pretty limiting, given that you have to book through Amex.

    Recent findings suggest that I think the issue is the steep annual fee, given that there are also much more affordable (and even no annual fee) cards with that kind of a rewards structure. In fairness, Amex doesn’t have another business card earning unlimited 2% cash back. It’s just not a upcoming concept more broadly, and there are lots of competing cards that I’d consider to be superior.

    So who should consider the card? As I see it, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is targeted at a specific demographic. This card could make sense for the following types of customers:.

    I do truly think this is a niche product. But the idea is that if you’re a small business owner charging hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars on credit cards per year, that annual fee won’t make much of a difference.

    Still, I’d like to compare this to some other popular products, as I think there are other cards that may be a better fit for some other people.

    In a recent development, perhaps the best direct comparison to the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is The American Express Blue Business Cash® Card (learn more). The card has no annual fee (Rates & Fees) and offers 2% cash back on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year (and 1% cash back thereafter).

    In a recent development, the upside here is obvious, as you’re earning 2% cash back with no fee. The downside is that the welcome offer is much smaller (though also with a smaller spending requirement), the card has foreign transaction fees, you’re capped at earning 2% cash back on the first $50,000 spent annually, and the card does have a preset spending limit.

    For a small business mostly spending money domestically, the Amex Blue Business Cash is a great alternative to the Amex Graphite Business Cash.

    Another potential alternative to the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is The Blue Business® Plus Credit Card from American Express (learn more). The card has no annual fee (Rates & Fees) and offers 2x Membership Rewards points on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year (and 1x points thereafter).

    If you’re good at redeeming points, that’s a pretty incredible return, since based on my latest miles & points valuations, Amex points are worth 1.7 cents each, for a return of up to 3.4%. The downsides to the Amex Blue Business Plus are otherwise identical to those on the Amex Blue Business Cash — the welcome offer is much smaller (though also with a smaller spending requirement), the card has foreign transaction fees, you’re capped at earning 2x points on the first $50,000 spent annually, and the card does have a preset spending limit.

    So the card is either useful if $50,000 covers your annual business spending, or you’re willing to use another card after you hit that initial $50,000 spending cap.

    Speaking of premium Amex business cards, it’s also worth comparing the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card to the American Express® Business Gold Card (learn more). The Amex Business Gold has a $375 annual fee (Rates & Fees), and offers an incredible rewards structure (with up to 4x Membership Rewards points in select categories), plus statement credits that can greatly help offset the annual fee.

    As I see it, the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card is the better option if you value cash back and a straightforward rewards structure, while the Amex Business Gold is the better option if you can take advantage of the bonus categories, and are willing to put in the effort to maximize points.

    While the above comparisons are all to Amex cards, I think it’s also worth comparing the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card to the Capital One Spark Cash Plus (learn more), as it’s perhaps the most direct competitor.

    In a recent development, the card has a massive welcome offer of $2,000 cash back after spending $30,000 within the first three months (plus an additional $2,000 cash back bonus for every $500,000 spent during the first year), offers 5% cash back on select Capital One Business Travel purchases and 2% cash back with no caps and no foreign transaction fees on other purchases, and it has a $150 annual fee. Furthermore, the card offers an annual bonus of $150 if you spend at least $150,000 on the card in a calendar year, essentially rebating the annual fee.

    I do think the Capital One Spark Cash Plus is more compelling than the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card on balance, unless you specifically have a reason you’d like an Amex, or value the statement credits tied to spending $250,000 per year.

    I’d also like to compare the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card to the Ink Business Premier® Credit Card (learn more), as it’s another potentially lucrative cash back card.

    Industry observers note that in addition to a substantial welcome offer of $1,000 cash back after spending $10,000 within the first three months, the card offers 5% cash back on Chase Travel purchases, 2.5% cash back on purchases of $5,000 or more, and 2% cash back on all other purchases, with no foreign transaction fees, and it has a $195 annual fee. So if you have a business that frequently makes large purchases, the Chase Ink Business Premier could be a great alternative.

    Recent findings suggest that the Amex Graphite Business Cash Card has a $295 annual fee, and offers unlimited 2% cash back, with no preset spending limit, plus a large welcome offer. The card also offers up to $2,400 in American Express One AP® statement credits, after spending $250,000 on eligible purchases on the card in a calendar year.

    Recent findings suggest that ultimately I’d consider this to be a niche card. The card could be worth getting for the excellent welcome offer, and it could be worth it if you have a business that spends a huge amount, and values the lack of a preset spending limit, the card’s Amex branding, and/or the statement credits.

    Beyond that, though, I tend to think there are better options. If you’re not a huge spender, the Amex Blue Business Cash and Amex Blue Business Plus are excellent options. If you’re willing to maximize points and bonus categories, consider the Amex Business Gold. And if you’re looking for the best direct alternative that’s arguably more lucrative, consider the Capital One Spark Cash Plus.

    Latest Update: Zinke PAC gave to family foundation he was investigated for

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1235 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025.
    • In a recent development, outgoing Montana GOP Rep.
    • According to recent reports, the gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, rep. Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    In a recent development, outgoing Montana GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.

    According to recent reports, the gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug. 31 from Zinke’s leadership political action committee to the nonprofit Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation, campaign finance records show. The donation is more than the foundation has reported receiving in any year since it was founded nearly two decades ago.

    Zinke’s wife, son, and sister right now serve on its board of directors, according to the foundation’s annual filing with the state of Montana.

    According to recent reports, in a brief interview, Zinke denied that any portion of the money transferred to the foundation will directly benefit him or any of his family members who sit on the board of directors. “No, no, never," he remarked when asked if any family members will draw a salary from the gift.

    The money will instead go to building a storage barn and kid’s sledding park on the property controlled by the foundation, Zinke noted.

    None of the records indicate Zinke violated the law or directly benefited from the gift to his foundation.

    “While it's not uncommon for a politician to transfer leftover money from a political war chest to charity, it is pretty rare for a politician to transfer leftover political funds to a charity that they or a relative controls,” said Michael Beckel, director of money in politics reform at Issue One, a bipartisan group that seeks to reduce influence of money in politics.

    Instead, outgoing members typically transfer remaining campaign cash to local party committees or candidates, Beckel added.

    Ethics experts say Zinke’s move highlights ongoing concerns over the broad latitude campaign finance law gives leadership PACs in how they spend money.

    “I definitely think it is something to be concerned about,” said Stuart McPhail, director of campaign finance litigation at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit watchdog.

    “Leadership PACs are really nothing more than personal slush funds under today's rules,” he said, noting that unlike regular campaign committees, member leadership PACs are not prohibited from donating to charities or organizations that could directly benefit the member or relative.

    Zinke, a former Navy SEAL who commanded special forces during the Iraq War, converted his traditional campaign committee to a leadership PAC — Commander Zinke Leadership Fund — in March 2026, shortly after announcing he would not run for reelection. It last reported having $1.4 million cash on hand in October of this year.

    It marks the second time one of Zinke’s political committees made a payment to the organization. In 2019, the committee Zinke ran during his earlier years in Congress — he served one term in the House before being tapped as Trump’s first-term Interior secretary — gave over $11,000 to the foundation before winding down operations.

    According to recent reports, the Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation was founded by Zinke and his wife in 2007 in his hometown of Whitefish, Mont., with plans to provide winter recreational activities for children. Its latest tax filing reports revenue of $15,000 and roughly equal expenses in 2024 for snow plowing and park maintenance.

    Zinke’s dealings with the organization were the subject of an ongoing inspector general investigation when he resigned as Interior secretary in January 2019.

    Investigators ultimately did not find that Zinke violated conflict-of-interest laws, but they concluded that he failed to comply with federal ethics obligations and “misused his official position in violation of federal regulations.” The Justice Department declined to prosecute Zinke.

    Zinke stepped down from the foundation in 2017, shortly after his Senate confirmation. But investigators found that he continued to represent the organization in negotiations with the developers of a commercial project adjacent to the foundation’s land and lied to an ethics agent about his involvement in the project.

    The project’s investors included David Lesar, then-chairman of oil services firm Halliburton.

    Another Zinke-tied leadership PAC has previously raised eyebrows in Washington.

    Industry observers note that supporting Electing American Leaders PAC — known as SEAL PAC — where Zinke serves as chairman, has been marred by accusations that it funneled money to political consultants instead of candidates. A 2022 CQ Roll Call analysis found that 87 percent of the PAC’s spending went to operating expenses.

    The PAC also made recurring monthly payments to a organization registered to Zinke’s son, Wolfgang Zinke, and based at a Zinke family-owned home in Whitefish.

    SEAL PAC’s executive director, Rob Catron, maintained that the payments constitute a consulting fee to Wolfgang Zinke for management of the PAC website, among other tasks. “He earns every penny of it,” Catron stated.

    Since May 2022, the PAC has given roughly $270,000 to Wolfgang Zinke’s organization, FG Solutions, for mailing and printing, records show — more than any individual candidate or committee supported by the PAC. The company also received $5,000 from a related super PAC, SEAL PAC USA, which can solicit unlimited contributions for independent expenditures but can’t donate directly to candidates.

    Montana corporate records show Wolfgang Zinke founded FG Solutions – which says it provides services including “personal assistant and any lawful purpose” – just 10 days before it received its first payment from the PAC in 2022.

    Catron defended how the PAC spends money on veterans running for the House, arguing that it takes money to raise money.

    “We raise a lion’s share of our funding through national direct mail fundraising, which is very expensive to do,” he noted, citing the PAC’s use of a national text message fundraising campaign as a major expense.

    Recent findings suggest that SEAL PAC raised about $9.6 million this election cycle, distributing about $1.1 million to GOP lawmakers and candidates, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Most of the committee's funds went to operating expenses, including over $3 million paid to Direct Support Services, a Washington-based vendor, for direct mail postage.

    Zinke’s not the only lawmaker to face scrutiny over how they spent surplus campaign cash in recent years.

    In 2023, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., set off alarm bells for transferring $200,000 from his campaign committee to The Sanders Institute, a nonprofit founded by his wife and stepson, following a $350,000 donation from his 2020 presidential campaign coffers.

    The organization briefly shut down during Sanders’ presidential run in 2019 to avoid the appearance of impropriety.

    Sanders’ stepson, David Driscoll — a former executive at Nike and snowboard manufacturer Burton — is listed on the think tank’s website as its executive director, drawing a six-figure annual salary according to tax filings.

    It’s unusual, though not unheard of, for campaign committees to pay family members of the candidate for bona fide work.

    “If [Wolfgang Zinke] is actually performing this work, he’s qualified to do it, and this is his typical market rate for this kind of contract, then it would be permissible, even if this was a campaign account,” McPhail stated about SEAL PAC's payments.

    But the payments could present a legal “gray area” over whether personal-use restrictions apply to certain PACs, according to McPhail.

    Miles with the lifemiles program don’t expire as long as you accrue some miles at least once every 12 months. Any mileage earning activity, including buying miles, will extend the expiration of your miles. However, redeeming miles as such doesn’t extend the expiration of your miles.

    If you’re looking to earn lifemiles, the good news is that there are lots of options beyond outright buying them.     #77201. Breaking: The 30 Finished Boeing 777-9s Parked In Washington That No Airline Wants To Fly

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1470 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: The 30 Finished Boeing 777-9s Parked In Washington That No Airline Wants To Fly

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1470 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Boeing 777X is finally beginning to look like a real aircraft rather than an endless certification project, with the 777-9 having been busy with its planned certification testing and Boeing still targeting first deliveries in 2027.
    • Industry observers note that all the while, regulators and Boeing continue working through the remaining Type Inspection Authorizations and the approvals needed for extended operations.
    • This is because the earliest production aircraft were built before the final production standard was established.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Boeing 777X is finally beginning to look like a real aircraft rather than an endless certification project, with the 777-9 having been busy with its planned certification testing and Boeing still targeting first deliveries in 2027. By the summer of 2026, the test fleet had accumulated more than 4,800 flight hours across roughly 1,700 flights.

    Industry observers note that all the while, regulators and Boeing continue working through the remaining Type Inspection Authorizations and the approvals needed for extended operations. However, the most interesting 777X story in 2026 is not the certification progress bar. It is the collection of more than 30 completed or substantially completed 777X airframes sitting at locations in Washington State, including Paine Field and Moses Lake.

    This is because the earliest production aircraft were built before the final production standard was established. Lufthansa, one of the program's launch customers, now wants Boeing to pay for accepting some of those airplanes, while Emirates has taken an even harder public line on the earliest examples.

    According to recent reports, the unusual situation exists because Boeing has been building customer aircraft while simultaneously completing the certification and production work needed to bring the 777-9 into commercial service. That is not necessarily unusual for a program of this scale, but the 777X program has taken so long to reach certification.

    This means that the gap between the earliest completed airframes and the final production configuration has become particularly significant. The result is a group of large, expensive widebodies that look ready to an observer on the ground but cannot simply be handed to an airline and flown into commercial service.

    In a recent development, reports indicate that more than 30 pre-standard 777-9 aircraft are parked while they await modifications needed to bring them closer to the configuration that Boeing ultimately intends to deliver. These aircraft are therefore not unwanted in the conventional sense, because airlines still want the 777-9 itself, but the earliest examples can carry a substantial financial and operational disadvantage.

    An airline taking one would effectively be accepting an aircraft that needs additional work before it becomes equivalent to a later production aircraft. That distinction explains why the headline about airlines refusing to fly the aircraft can be misleading.

    According to recent reports, lufthansa has not rejected the 777-9 program, and it still has 20 examples on order. Instead, the Star Alliance carrier's Chief Executive Officer Carsten Spohr has said the airline is discussing with Boeing which early-built aircraft it will accept and which it will not, with financial compensation required if Lufthansa takes aircraft that need to be modernized.

    Boeing's certification updates provide a much more encouraging picture than the parked aircraft might suggest. In July, the firm said that the 777-9 had completed 50% of its planned certification testing, with more than 4,800 flight-test hours and roughly 1,700 flights accumulated by the test fleet.

    Industry observers note that boeing also noted that most Type Inspection Authorizations had been granted, leaving further approvals, including those associated with ETOPS demonstrations, among the crucial remaining steps. The Boeing 777-9 is now in the later stages of its certification campaign, with Boeing describing the program as focused on closing remaining regulatory requirements rather than discovering whether the aircraft fundamentally works.

    Industry observers note that in August, Boeing flew both the 777-9 and 737 MAX 10 through naturally occurring icing conditions. Rather than relying entirely on simulated environments, Boeing's teams searched for clouds containing supercooled water and deliberately positioned the aircraft where ice could accumulate on important aerodynamic surfaces.

    Industry observers note that the 777-9 completed an 8.5-hour flight, while the 737 MAX 10 spent six hours in the relevant conditions. The testing was designed to examine how the airplanes handled with ice accumulating on the wings, horizontal stabilizers, vertical stabilizers, and other critical areas, with Boeing targeting roughly one to two inches of ice during parts of the campaign.

    Sources indicate that meteorologists monitored weather systems and helped crews locate suitable conditions, while onboard instrumentation measured the environment and the aircraft's response. Such testing illustrates why certification can take years even after an aircraft has already completed thousands of hours of development flying.

    For the Boeing 777-9, the result was encouraging, with test pilots reporting that the aircraft maintained its expected handling characteristics in the icing environment. The aircraft's handling remained consistent enough that the icing would have been difficult to notice without the flight-test instrumentation. That is good news for Boeing, but it does not remove the separate problem involving aircraft already built before the final production standard was established.

    Lufthansa is particularly important because it is set to be the 777-9's launch customer and has a direct interest in receiving aircraft as soon as possible without inheriting an avoidable modernization bill. Spohr has confirmed that the airline is in discussions with Boeing over which of the first-built 777-9s it will accept.

    He has also explicitly linked acceptance of aircraft requiring later modernization to financial compensation from Boeing. The airline's position closely resembles that of Emirates, which has publicly expressed reluctance to accept the earliest 777-9 examples because of the amount of work needed to bring them to final production standard.

    In a recent development, spohr acknowledged that Lufthansa has been less public about the issue but stated the situation is essentially the same. For airlines, the concern is not simply whether an early aircraft can eventually be made compliant, but whether taking it creates additional downtime, engineering work, maintenance complexity, and uncertainty compared with receiving a later-built aircraft. That is why Boeing's compensation discussions matter.

    If an airline accepts an early-production aircraft and Boeing covers the modernization costs, the aircraft can still become a useful part of the fleet. Without compensation, however, the airline would be absorbing the consequences of receiving an aircraft whose configuration reflects the long development process of the 777X program. Lufthansa's comments therefore suggest the parked aircraft are becoming as much a commercial negotiation as a manufacturing problem.

    The 777X was supposed to enter service years ago, and that long delay has created an unusual production challenge. Boeing has continued developing the aircraft, conducting certification testing and preparing production airplanes while the regulatory process stretched far beyond the original schedule.

    As a result, Boeing completed some aircraft before it knew exactly what the final certified configuration would require. That creates a difficult choice for Boeing: leaving the aircraft parked preserves them while the company works through the necessary changes, but every month they remain on the ground adds storage, maintenance, and financing costs.

    It has been revealed that sending them to customers without the appropriate modifications would create an equally difficult problem, because airlines would have to schedule the additional work and potentially accept lower utilization from brand new aircraft. The reported fleet of more than 30 parked aircraft therefore represents both a liability and a sign of how far the program has progressed.

    Boeing would not have dozens of customer-bound 777Xs sitting around if it were still at the early design stage, but it also would not need extensive rework if the earliest production airplanes already matched the final standard. The aircraft are caught between those two realities, waiting for the certification and industrial processes to catch up with their physical completion.

    Despite the controversy surrounding the first aircraft, little evidence suggests airlines have abandoned the 777-9 itself. More than 650 777X aircraft have been ordered between the three variants, making the program one of the industry's most key future widebody families.

    Lufthansa remains committed to its 20-aircraft order, while Emirates has an order for 235 777-9s plus 35 777-8s, showing that the industry's largest customers still see a role for the aircraft. The reason is straightforward: the 777-9 offers airlines a combination of size, range and efficiency that fits the upper end of the long-haul market, particularly as carriers replace older four-engine aircraft and earlier-generation 777s.

    Recent findings suggest that airlines therefore have a strong incentive to wait for the program rather than abandon it, even if they would prefer not to receive the earliest production examples. The commercial disagreement is about which aircraft should arrive first and who should pay to make them ready, not necessarily about whether the aircraft has a future. Lufthansa's own contingency planning shows how seriously airlines are treating the delivery schedule.

    Industry observers note that spohr has said the airline has prepared for both a scenario in which the 777-9 arrives as planned and one in which further delays require older aircraft to remain in service, including the possible reactivation of older A340-300s. For Boeing, then, the next challenge is not simply getting the 777-9 certified: it is turning a backlog of early-built aircraft into acceptable assets while delivering a production standard that airlines are prepared to put into everyday service.

    Sources indicate that jetBlue is presently offering a limited time 125% bonus on purchased points. With this, TrueBlue members can purchase points for as little as 1.43 cents each. Is this a good deal?

    Let’s take a look at the details — so that I don’t bury the lede, let me say that I’d only recommend taking advantage of this JetBlue buy points offer with a specific use in mind, and primarily if you intend to redeem on partner airlines.

    Link: Buy JetBlue TrueBlue points with this promotion with a 125% bonus.

    Between 12AM ET on November 18 and 11:59PM ET on December 31, 2026, JetBlue TrueBlue is offering a bonus on purchased points, which is close to being in line with the best offers from the program.

    JetBlue TrueBlue is offering up to a 125% bonus on purchasing points. The offer is structured as follows, with three tiers of bonuses:.

    JetBlue ordinarily allows TrueBlue members to purchase up to 200,000 points per calendar year. However, during this promotion, that cap has been increased to 300,000 points.

    Sources indicate that jetBlue ordinarily charges 3.0 cents per purchased point, before the 7.5% federal excise tax. After factoring in the federal excise tax, the standard cost is 3.225 cents per purchased point.

    With this JetBlue points sale, you’d pay the following amounts per purchased point, factoring in the bonus:.

    If you wanted to purchase the fewest possible points at the best possible price, you’d want to purchase a total of 45,000 points (20,000 points plus 25,000 bonus points) at a cost of $645, which gets you the cost of 1.43 cents per point, including all taxes.

    Meanwhile if you wanted to purchase the most possible points, you’d want to purchase a total of 675,000 points (300,000 points plus 375,000 bonus points) at a cost of $9,675, which gets you the same cost per point.

    Officially, JetBlue states that it can take up to 72 hours for purchased points to post. However, in practice (based on my test experience of buying points), they’ll typically post almost instantly. There’s no guarantee of that, though.

    Note that the purchase of JetBlue points is non-refundable, so only make a purchase if you have a specific use in mind. Furthermore, the purchase of JetBlue points doesn’t count toward Mosaic elite status, in case that’s a consideration.

    When JetBlue does offer a promotion on purchased points, it’s typically in the range of 120-130%. So this is within that range. Personally I’d buy points based on when you’re ready to redeem them, rather than the exact cost. After all, the cost to buy points with a 120% bonus vs. 125% bonus vs. 130% bonus doesn’t differ that much.

    Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the program, before this one.

    JetBlue TrueBlue points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. That means if you use a JetBlue credit card to pay for your purchase, it wouldn’t code as a JetBlue purchase.

    It has been revealed that therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. See my guide to the best credit cards for buying points.

    JetBlue TrueBlue has become more interesting on the redemption front in recent years, and there are definitely some ways to get outsized value. For that matter, in some cases people may find value in topping off their points balance, in order to have enough points for a redemption.

    Let’s look at the opportunities to redeem TrueBlue points, first for travel on JetBlue, and then for travel on partner airlines. For what it’s worth, based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider TrueBlue points to be worth 1.3 cents each.

    When it comes to redeeming on JetBlue, TrueBlue is a revenue based frequent flyer program. That means the cost of an award redemption is correlated to how much a ticket would cost in cash, though it’s not always a consistent cent per point value.

    In my experience, you’ll typically get around 1.3-1.5 cents per TrueBlue point toward the cost of a ticket on JetBlue in economy.

    In a recent development, just as an example, take a JetBlue flight from Boston to Fort Lauderdale, which costs $334 if paying cash. If redeeming TrueBlue points, you’d pay 22,500 points plus $5.60 in taxes & fees, meaning you’re getting around 1.46 cents of value per point.

    Industry observers note that as another example, take a JetBlue flight from Boston to San Francisco, which has both economy and Mint business class. If paying cash, you’d pay $198 or $676. If redeeming points, you’d pay 14,200 points or 47,300 points, plus $5.60 in taxes & fees, meaning you’re getting around 1.35-1.42 cents of value per point.

    As you can see, these are situations where you probably shouldn’t buy TrueBlue points. For example, there’s no reason to acquire 14,200 points for 1.43 cents each, for a total cost of $203 (plus the $5.60 in taxes & fees), when you could instead just outright buy the ticket for $198.

    One thing to keep in mind is that if you have JetBlue’s most premium card, you can get a 15% award rebate, so maybe there is a little upside there.

    Sources indicate that jetBlue TrueBlue has gotten better about adding redemptions on partner airlines in recent times, including on Qatar Airways, Condor, and United Airlines. We’re also now seeing redemptions added on China Airlines. There’s definitely some value to be had here.

    It has been revealed that for example, you could redeem just 47,400 points for Condor business class one-way from Frankfurt to Toronto. That’s an amazing opportunity to buy points and immediately get outsized value.

    As another example, you could redeem 29,600 points for Qatar Airways business class one-way from Munich to Doha. Given the points acquisition costs we’re talking about, that’s an amazing value.

    One caveat I’d just like to add is that partner award availability can be really tough to come by, so only buy points if you have an understanding of what that availability is like.

    It has been revealed that as I see it, the decision of whether to buy points from a particular loyalty program comes down both to how valuable that currency is, and it also comes down to how many ways there are to acquire the currency. So that’s why it’s worth mentioning that JetBlue TrueBlue points are really easy to acquire.

    At this point, JetBlue partners with virtually all transferable points currencies, so you can earn TrueBlue points through Amex Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One Rewards, Chase Ultimate Rewards, Citi ThankYou, Wells Fargo, etc. Bilt, Chase, Citi, and Wells Fargo, have 1:1 transfer ratios, while Amex has a 5:4 ratio, and Capital One has a 5:3 ratio.

    Another option is to apply for JetBlue’s co-branded credit cards, which often have large welcome bonuses. Those points of course won’t post anywhere close to instantly, but it’s a good strategy for building up your TrueBlue points balance over time.

    So there’s no shortage of opportunities to earn TrueBlue points — it’s just a function of whether you’d rather part with cash or a points currency.

    • Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the new year, making the most of their coming majority.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February. He will be a key player in leading oversight efforts next year — and so will Democratic staff. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the new year, making the most of their coming majority.

    Recent findings suggest that that means staffing up major committees. And for the dozens of attorneys and other aides preparing to take on a belligerent Trump administration that has cast Democratic oversight as potentially criminal, the job will come with extra scrutiny.

    Arya Hariharan, former chief oversight counsel to Sen. Richard J. Durbin on the Senate Judiciary Committee and now a partner at Holland & Knight, remarked the pressure will be on from day one.

    “Are you prepared to not sleep very much and know that every single thing you do is going to be scrutinized, every footnote, every comma?” Hariharan stated.

    In a recent development, still, the way Hariharan sees it, serving on the Hill is worth it. “I hope they all fall in love with it because it’s a lovely place to work,” she says of staffers headed there for the first time.

    Recent findings suggest that the work done by attorneys and other staff in oversight probes can quickly become part of constitutional law. When Trump adviser Peter Navarro defied a subpoena from Democrats investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, it touched off debates about executive privilege and contempt of Congress. Probes of Hunter Biden led to similar court fights.

    Some questions have gone all the way up to the Supreme Court, like in Trump v. Mazars, when the House fought to access Trump’s business records during his first administration in furtherance of toughening up government ethics laws.

    There’s every indication that pressure will continue in the new Congress. James Melendres, a partner at Snell & Wilmer, noted Democrats are poised for aggressive oversight efforts, even if they know it could be tough to make headway against litigation resistant administration officials.

    According to recent reports, “Democrats are going to have less than two years to show results. I think they are going to move really fast,” Melendres stated.

    Democrats will likely soon start to send out preservation letters to private companies, institutions and others they intend to probe in the fresh year, if they haven’t already, Melendres noted.

    “There may be significant pushback from the administration, from agencies and individual government officials who receive requests. I think third-party, nongovernment agencies and individuals are going to be high on the list for these committees,” he remarked.

    Sources indicate that in addition to the hiring that happens over the next few weeks, House Democrats will have major decisions to make about chamber and committee rules for the new Congress, including who will hold subpoena authority. And off-Hill observers will be watching closely.

    “For companies, for individuals and their counsel, mapping all of that is going to be a big part of the job between now and early January,” Melendres said.

    Lawmakers need to nail down funding levels for congressional committees and staff — the amount of money involved can make a significant difference in how big investigations get. Major committees, and major investigations, take a large amount of staff and expertise to get going.

    According to recent reports, for instance, the special House panel that investigated the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol spent about $14 million in less than 18 months, including for dozens of staffers.

    In a recent development, standing committees, such as Oversight and Judiciary, take a good chunk of change, too. In 2025 the House spent $12.9 million on the House Oversight and Government Reform panel, and $13.1 million on the House Judiciary Committee.

    Those expenditures mean dozens of staff working long hours to review documents, send letters, send subpoenas and conduct interviews. Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is expected to serve as chair next year, noted he wouldn’t get into specifics yet about how many resources the fresh Congress may devote to oversight efforts.

    “But we are talking about the most corrupt administration in the history of the United States, and this is an overwhelming and daunting task that faces us,” Raskin remarked.

    The Trump administration itself has already signaled it intends to push back forcefully on congressional oversight efforts.

    Earlier this month, President Donald Trump described Democrats’ vows to investigate his administration as “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”.

    Days later, the White House counsel sent a letter saying that subpoena threats from House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and others “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”.

    U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz for the Southern District of Texas followed up with letters of his own to Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.; Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.; and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., urging them to preserve documents tied to their promised oversight.

    “The American people are entitled to freely associate without their elected officials terrorizing them with aggressive, harassing government action,” Reitz’s letter to Warren stated.

    Members of the incoming majority have signaled they intend to defend themselves and their probes, and Blumenthal noted he won’t be deterred by the letter.

    Recent findings suggest that “There’s no way that I’m going to be intimidated or bullied. It would be laughable and ludicrous, but it is a clear abuse and misuse of prosecutorial powers and weaponization by the Department of Justice,” mentioned Blumenthal, who serves as the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

    As for Raskin, he called the White House counsel letter and other missives “absurd on its face.”.

    “I’m sure they would love to get into a whole series of letters and counter-letters and litigation. They’re trying to distract everybody from the fact that they just lost the worst landslide electoral repudiation in at least a half century in America, and so they’re going to pick a fight,” Raskin told reporters.

    Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely incoming speaker, told reporters last week that he intended oversight efforts in his chamber to be led by Raskin and Garcia.

    “We haven’t ruled anything in. We haven’t ruled anything out. We’re going to follow the facts. We’re going to apply the law. We’re going to be guided by the Constitution, and we’re going to let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries noted.

    Democrats have already publicly listed a handful of job postings for oversight staff and counsel, ranging from the Science to Armed Services to Judiciary panels, set to start early next year.

    Recent findings suggest that beyond those hires, House Democrats will have to make one major pick they haven’t yet unveiled — the House counsel. The position, first created in the 1970s, is hired by the majority and advocates for the chamber in court. That attorney, along with a group of bipartisan House leaders controlled by the majority, will steer the chamber’s legal strategy.

    In prior Democratic Congresses, that office has been active in court; Doug Letter frequently argued on behalf of the Democratic House majority seeking to enforce subpoenas on behalf of congressional committees. The position is held by Matthew Berry in the current Republican-controlled House.

    “I mean, I think a lot of people are interested in that job,” Raskin remarked.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Travelers are conditioned to expect high prices at airport retailers and restaurants, so over $5 for a bottle of water at an airport shop, or $25 for a burger at a mediocre airport restaurant, might not catch anyone off guard.
    • However, did you know there are caps on how much retailers at airports are supposed to be able to charge, and they’re largely just not enforced?
    • Industry observers note that airports generate revenue in a variety of ways, and one of the major ways is through the retailers they have in the terminal.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Travelers are conditioned to expect high prices at airport retailers and restaurants, so over $5 for a bottle of water at an airport shop, or $25 for a burger at a mediocre airport restaurant, might not catch anyone off guard.

    However, did you know there are caps on how much retailers at airports are supposed to be able to charge, and they’re largely just not enforced? Well, or perhaps more accurately, they are enforced, but using very dishonest math. The backstory of this is interesting.

    Industry observers note that airports generate revenue in a variety of ways, and one of the major ways is through the retailers they have in the terminal. An airport is like a shopping mall with a very captive audience, and as you’d expect, rent for businesses in airports is absolutely through the roof, as a result of that.

    According to recent reports, but in order to balance things out and prevent retailers from exploiting consumers, over 80% of airports in the United States specifically stipulate the maximum prices that airports can charge consumers. These terms are typically baked into the contracts that airport retailers sign, and failure to adhere to the rules can lead to consequences, at least in theory.

    The airports with pricing caps for airport businesses generally fall into one of two categories:.

    It has been revealed that if there are supposed to be rules in place capping airport pricing, then why is this such a widespread issue? More Perfect Union recently published a great video investigating this issue, and it’s a fascinating watch. First they actually analyze airport pricing, and then they confront airport authorities about the lack of enforcement.

    Here’s what’s interesting — airport retailers do have to submit comparisons for benchmark pricing, to prove that they’re not violating rules and exploiting customers. The matter is what kind of businesses are considered comparable for the purposes of “street pricing.”.

    For example, 9NEWS recently investigated this at Denver Airport, finding that a basic Starbucks coffee cost $4.55 in the airport, compared to $2.95 outside the airport (a 54% markup), and a bag of cashews cost $9.99 in the airport, compared to $4.74 outside the airport (a 110% markup).

    The airport’s VP of Concessions agreed to sit down with the reporter to discuss this, and she remarked the results of his investigation were great news — she suggested that 93% of the prices were compliant, and said “that’s pretty darn good.” How could that be, given the high markups compared to nearby businesses?

    The issue boils down to how much latitude businesses have to submit pricing comparisons:.

    What’s wild is how the airport official responds to Starbucks just having consistent pricing, and violating the rules:.

    Industry observers note that VP of Concessions: “What I get from that is, they’re looking for consistency, across the board, across the nation, across the world.”Reporter: “I can’t help but think that travelers may be looking for consistency, but if they see a cheaper cup of coffee, they’ll probably be okay with it.”VP of Concessions: “I don’t know the answer to that. This is how we take care of our passengers, by ensuring that they are paying fair and transparent pricing, while supporting our business partners.”.

    Back to the original story, the More Perfect Union reporter confronted the Port Authority of Newly introduced York and New Jersey about pricing like $6.89 for one liter of Smart Water, compared to closer to $3.50 at nearby bodegas.

    The response was that “comparing a Hudson to a bodega isn’t appropriate,” because “Hudson is a specialty market.” The approved price comparison was reportedly based on the price of water at Tablet Works, a “wellness & concierge pharmacy” in a high-end mall.

    The other thing to keep in mind is that a large percentage of airport retailers and restaurants are run by the same few companies, like HMSHost, which is a subsidiary of Avolta. So clearly they have a centralized approach to submitting pricing comparisons, and know exactly what they’re doing. Interestingly, the few independent businesses in some airports were found to have the most honest pricing.

    According to recent reports, so to sum it up, the system is designed to be rigged. Airport authorities can technically pretend they’re looking out for consumers by setting a cap. Retailers can submit pricing comparisons to the highest prices they can find anywhere. Then airport authorities verify those prices to pretend they’re doing their jobs.

    It has been revealed that airports are obviously complicit in all of this. They make money by charging sky high rent, and the reason they can do that is because retailers can charge hugely inflated prices. The more profits retailers make, the more airports can charge in rent. And they know that no consumer is going to avoid an airport because of high concession costs.

    Around 80% of airports in the United States cap the prices that retailers can charge, so in most cases, you’re not supposed to be paying more than 15% above “street pricing.” The issue is the liberties that businesses can take with what constitutes “street pricing.”.

    According to recent reports, the price of the bottle of water or smoothie you’re buying isn’t compared to what you’d pay at a nearby gas station and smoothie shop, but instead, is being compared to what you’d pay at Erewhon. Talk about a very broken system, with no incentives for any party to actually be honest….

    What do you make of this airport pricing situation?

    #77196. The Plot to Overthrow the Electoral College Must Fail

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1619 w)
