    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nationalreview ↗ Open Full Page

    The Plot to Overthrow the Electoral College Must Fail

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1619 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that article II, Section 1 of the Constitution sets out the process by which Americans select their president.
    • In a recent development, democrats have been railing against the Electoral College since losing the 2000 and 2016 elections while winning a plurality of the popular vote.
    • Sources indicate that A proposed workaround has sailed through the legislatures of 18 blue states and the District of Columbia: the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that article II, Section 1 of the Constitution sets out the process by which Americans select their president. Alexander Hamilton marveled at the time, in Federalist No. 68, that it was “almost the only part of the system, of any consequence, which has escaped without severe censure, or which has received the slightest mark of approbation from its opponents.” The core of that process is that the members of the Electoral College are selected in each state. With only the Twelfth Amendment’s modification in 1804 to adjust how the vice president is selected, this same system has been in continuous use for 238 years. It is how George Washington, Abraham Lincoln, Franklin D. Roosevelt, Ronald Reagan, and Barack Obama were elected. Now, a nefarious plot aims to overthrow the American system.

    In a recent development, democrats have been railing against the Electoral College since losing the 2000 and 2016 elections while winning a plurality of the popular vote. These partisan sour grapes have often been dismissed as empty talk because the Electoral College is established by the Constitution, so only an amendment could abolish it. An amendment requires a two-thirds vote of Congress and the consent of 38 states, both of which are out of reach on a party-line vote.

    Sources indicate that A proposed workaround has sailed through the legislatures of 18 blue states and the District of Columbia: the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact. The theory is that these states would award their electors not to the winner of the popular vote in their own state, but to the winner of the national popular vote. It may be that a state can decide on its own to do this. States have not always picked electors by statewide popular vote. Many states at the Founding had their state legislatures choose electors. South Carolina did so all the way to the Civil War. Colorado in 1876 was the last state to do so, but only because it had just been admitted to statehood and claimed not to have time to organize a statewide vote. Other states have awarded electors to the winners of each House district, as Maine and Nebraska do today; this system was upheld by the Supreme Court in 1892.

    Industry observers note that but the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact is not just a unilateral decision by individual states about how to award their electors. If it had been, it would already have been effective in 2024, and Donald Trump would have won the Electoral College 530–8 with 49.7 percent of the popular vote. Instead, it is styled as an agreement that goes into effect only if states composing a majority of the Electoral College approve it. At present, the signatories control 222 electoral votes. With Democrats gaining trifectas in Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Nevada, and Arizona, they conceivably could pass the compact in states controlling 283 electoral votes. They also now control the New Hampshire state legislature, although with a veto-proof majority only in one of its two chambers, they would have to get through Republican Governor Kelly Ayotte.

    Industry observers note that passage is not certain. Michigan Democrats have previously rejected the compact in 2023 and 2024, and in Nevada (a smaller state that would be swamped under the compact), the Democratic governor vetoed it in 2019. Some of the small-state signatories, such as Delaware, Vermont, Rhode Island, or New Mexico, might yet have second thoughts now that they are playing with live ammunition.

    Moreover, under Article I, Section 10, interstate compacts require the consent of Congress. Even if Democrats passed it in the next two years with the aim of changing the rules for the 2028 election, Trump would surely veto it. After the 2030 Census, a number of the signatory states are expected to lose House seats, which will further narrow the margin for keeping it in effect. Then, there’s the question of whether the Supreme Court would allow individual states to gang up and effectively nullify the entire constitutional design of our presidential election system.

    Legal obstacles aside, this is a bad idea. To start with, the very durability of our system over such a long period is an argument in its favor. No other nation has used the same system for choosing its head of state and government for so long. Leaving aside the dubious precedents of 1824 (when popular vote records were not kept in the most populous state) and 1876 (when fraud was rampant in both parties and Southern Democrats engaged in mass violence against Republican voters), the Electoral College has only delivered a different outcome from the national popular vote three times in our history. In each case, the national vote was fairly close and neither candidate got a popular majority, so the Electoral College provided the legitimacy of a majority result that the popular vote could not. This may have frustrated Californians, but it was not just the tyranny of a few small places with no people in them. In 2016, Trump won the popular vote in seven of the ten largest states. It is nearly impossible to win a national popular majority without carrying the Electoral College.

    Sources indicate that we have an Electoral College because we are a nation of diverse and distinct states. The American people are long accustomed to this system. The people ratified the Constitution and its amendments state-by-state. The Senate is elected by the people in states, the House by people in districts. Both political parties choose their presidential nominees by primary elections in each state. Americans have never before held a nationwide popular vote for any purpose. Our election systems, run by state and local officials with a variety of rules for the timing of casting and counting ballots and for confirming the qualifications of voters, are not designed for such a vote.

    According to recent reports, our campaigns today still prioritize appeals to the most closely divided states. This encourages presidential candidates to pitch at least some of their message to voters in the center, and also to travel the country in order to garner coverage in statewide media and the support of state and local power brokers. A national popular vote campaign would drive us even further down the road of nationalizing the campaign media environment and encouraging candidates to rally voters in their party’s strongholds. It would also exacerbate the divide between urban and rural or small-town America, given how the largest cities could effectively ally themselves against their own in-state neighbors.

    In a recent development, few of the world’s democracies conduct a nationwide vote for the chief executive. In France, which is one of those, the first man to win such a vote seized power in a coup before his first term ended. National popular plebiscites are far more common in dictatorial systems, where the president has more control over who counts the votes. One of the reasons why the January 6 mob was never a serious threat to overturn the 2020 election was that the state-by-state winners had already been publicly certified in 50 separate state capitals. This was a deliberate feature of the system: As Hamilton wrote, “as the electors, chosen in each State, are to assemble and vote in the State in which they are chosen, this detached and divided situation will expose them much less to heats and ferments . . . than if they were all to be convened at one time, in one place.”.

    In a recent development, we would inevitably need to overhaul our entire election system to accommodate a nationwide vote. It is not a coincidence that such a nationalization of elections is favored by many of the same people who want to do away with the Electoral College. As things stand today, the whole country would have to wait on California, which not only takes weeks to count votes, but does so in order to count late-arriving ballots and to “cure” defective ballots — a process bound to erode confidence in a close election. That matters little when nobody doubts the outcome in California. But by making elections turn on the margins of victory in the deepest-blue or deepest-red jurisdictions, whose election officials are uniformly of the same party, the incentives for all manner of electoral malfeasance would be supercharged.

    It has been revealed that the 1888 election provides a vivid, if extreme, example of how the Electoral College limits the scope of mischief done by the corruption of voting systems in particular states. The eleven states of the former Confederacy were then well into the post-Reconstruction suppression of the black vote in their states. As a result, the Democratic nominee, Grover Cleveland, won those states by almost 25 points, with over 60 percent of the vote. This propelled Cleveland to a narrow plurality in the national popular vote even though his Republican opponent, Benjamin Harrison, won a popular majority in the rest of the country. Yet the Electoral College gave Harrison the victory because his support was not as concentrated in an unrepresentative handful of states in which the vote was compromised.

    If a nationwide vote would be a headache, a nationwide recount would be a nightmare. Nobody who lived through the 2000 and 2020 post-election controversies should have any illusions that such a thing could be conducted in a civil and orderly fashion in today’s America. Rather than wait to learn that lesson the hard way, we should step back from the brink of overthrowing the system that has chosen our nation’s leader from the beginning.

    The Editors comprise the senior editorial staff of National Review magazine and nationalreview.com.

    On “The Plot to Overthrow the Electoral College Must Fail”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Emirates is known for being a world-class airline, though at this point, the carrier’s ground experience at Dubai International Airport (DXB) leaves a lot to be desired, especially for premium passengers.

    While I don’t want to suggest that the carrier’s first class lounges and business class lounges are terrible, they’re far from cutting edge, and the design definitely feels extremely outdated. Earlier this year, I wrote a post asking if Emirates was going to revamp its lounges at the airport, or just wait until the theoretical move to Dubai World Central (DWC) around 2032.

    In a recent development, well, it seems that my concerns have now been addressed, as Emirates has announced plans to completely transform its lounge experience in Dubai. Over the summer we saw the airline start to roll out a upcoming global lounge concept for outstation lounges, and that idea is now coming to Dubai as well.

    As is the case for any airline, rolling out a upcoming lounge concept at a hub airport isn’t easy, given that it requires spaces to be closed. So that’s why it’s worth noting that Emirates is taking an innovative approach to refreshing its lounges in Dubai:.

    In a recent development, emirates is investing a total of 400 million AED ($109 million) in these lounge spaces. Interestingly, Emirates claims that “all flagship lounges” will be getting a redesign, though there’s zero mention of the lounges in Concourse A, which are the biggest lounges in the world (they span the entire concourse), and offer direct boarding to planes. So it’s not clear when those lounges will undergo updates.

    Here’s how Emirates President Tim Clark describes this development:.

    Sources indicate that “Our customers expect the very best from Emirates, whether while flying or spending time with us on the ground. We believe the airport experience should be every bit as exceptional as the journey itself, and that’s why we are transforming our lounges globally. This new First Class Lounge in Dubai is the first taste of what’s to come. And if these are the lengths we will go to for a temporary lounge… just imagine what you can expect from new Emirates Lounges going forward. Over the next two years, we’ll be unveiling a completely different lounge experience, with new concepts in dining, wellness, entertainment and personalised hospitality. We’re going well beyond a traditional refurbishment and creating extraordinary spaces.”.

    In a recent development, we’ve already seen how Emirates is overhauling its global lounge network, and I’d say the changes are pretty awesome. So what can we expect in Dubai? As you can see, Clark references how the temporary upcoming first class lounge is just a small glimpse into what we can expect in the future. Below is a video showing the new concept, and I must say, it looks impressive!

    Here’s how Emirates describes the lounge concept, broadly:.

    Featuring immersive culinary experiences to dedicated wellness facilities and innovative entertainment concepts, Emirates is redefining what customers can expect from their time at the airport. Building on Emirates’ renowned hospitality, customers can expect distinct spaces for dining, relaxation, work and socialising – complemented by intuitive technology, refined interiors and elevated personal service. Each lounge will bear the hallmarks of the iconic Emirates brand, with the interiors conveying luxury, comfort, exceptional hospitality and global appeal.

    When it comes to the temporary latest first class lounge, here are the details:.

    Industry observers note that as much as people like to suggest that Gulf carriers just throw money down the drain when it comes to passenger experience, Emirates is actually a pretty disciplined and cost focused business, which is also clear based on the fact that the airline still has angled business class seats with seven seats per row. 😉.

    It has been revealed that but when the airline does invest and upgrade its products, it has a pretty good sense of what customers like. Barista coffee, Dom Perignon, and a gym? Count me in (though maybe the amenities shouldn’t be enjoyed in that order). 😉 It does sound like there still won’t be dedicated bedrooms, which would be disappointing, but also wouldn’t surprise me, given the volume of rooms they’d need to serve guests.

    Two things stand out to me here:.

    Emirates is hugely investing in its lounge network in Dubai, something that’s long overdue, if you ask me. Over the next two years, at least four lounges will be getting a full makeover, to match the carrier’s latest lounge aesthetic.

    Industry observers note that we’ve just seen the opening of a new temporarily first class lounge in Concourse B, which is described as an example of what’s to come. Next year that lounge is expected to become a business class lounge, as a new flagship first class lounge opens, along with additional first and business class lounges.

    The upcoming design aesthetic looks great, and it sounds like some thought is being put into amenities as well. I look forward to seeing this transformation, though I can’t help but wonder if this reflects a delay with Emirates moving to its new hub airport.

    What do you make of Emirates’ latest lounge concept?

    #77194. Industry News: How To Fly Without A License In America

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1480 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: How To Fly Without A License In America

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1480 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that gaining a pilot's license can be costly and prohibitive for many, including for those who just want to fly in a hang glider or ultralight aircraft.
    • It has been revealed that when the FAA drafted Part 103 in 1982, it drew a hard line.
    • Sources indicate that flying is extremely regulated, and pilots are required to have licenses to fly aircraft.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that gaining a pilot's license can be costly and prohibitive for many, including for those who just want to fly in a hang glider or ultralight aircraft. The FAA created an exemption on the premise that a vehicle light and slow enough poses minimal kinetic risk to people and property on the ground. It ruled that pilots of these aircraft, subject to strict parameters, can be mostly free of its regulations. This allows some people to enjoy the thrill of flying without having to worry about regulatory red tape.

    It has been revealed that when the FAA drafted Part 103 in 1982, it drew a hard line. It set tight restrictions on the weight and speed of the aircraft and then permitted the pilot to not be regulated at all. Other countries have gone in a different direction, requiring basic pilot training and registration and relaxing the limitations on the aircraft. Here is what to know about legally flying in the United States without a pilot's license or medical certificate.

    Sources indicate that flying is extremely regulated, and pilots are required to have licenses to fly aircraft. But as with many things in life, it's not quite that simple, and there are allowances on the margins. The FAA’s Part 103 rules let you fly an “ultralight vehicle” with no pilot certificate, medical, registration, or airworthiness certificate.

    The FAA explains, "Pilots of ultralight vehicles subject to Part 103 are not required to have training or previous experience prior to the operation of these vehicles. You should consider receiving adequate training prior to participation." How the aircraft is advertised does not override FAA regulations. The vehicle may be advertised as "powered ultralight," "hang glider," or "hang balloon", but its weight and performance determine how it is classified under FAA rules.

    Buyers are encouraged to be aware of aircraft advertised as meeting the requirements for use as an ultralight vehicle, but do not. Being within Part 103 means operators are not required to have a student, sport, or private pilot license, nor are they legally required to log flight hours or pass an FAA written or practical checkride. A checkride is the practical test a pilot takes to earn a new certificate, rating, or to maintain proficiency.

    To qualify as an ultralight vehicle, the aircraft must be single-seat and, if it is powered, it must weigh under 254 lb (115 kg) empty with no more than five gallons (19 liters) of fuel. Its speed is capped at 55 knots at full power and a 24-knot stall speed. Unpowered ultralights, such as hang gliders, must weigh under 155 lb (70 kg). Balloons and gliders are considered unpowered vehicles.

    Industry observers note that if the ultralight exceeds these limits, it is deemed to be an aircraft and requires a registration and a certified pilot. An ultralight also cannot be operated under Part 103 if it has been issued a current US or foreign airworthiness certificate. Flying within Part 103 limits operations to daylight only and prohibits operating within congested areas. This includes areas where people have assembled (e.g., a stadium).

    Unpowered ultralight (glider/balloon).

    Single-seat only (no passengers).

    Single-seat only (no passengers).

    No US or foreign airworthiness certificate.

    No US or foreign airworthiness certificate.

    In a recent development, pilots operating aircraft under Part 103 are still required to keep ultralights separated from commercial traffic and populated areas. Ultralights are permitted to fly freely in Class G (uncontrolled airspace), but are prohibited from Class B, C, D, or surface-level Class E airspace unless the pilot obtains prior authorization. They must also yield the right of way to all conventional aircraft. Weather conditions are required to be reasonably clear with visual reference to the surface.

    In a recent development, due to the strict empty weight and stall speed limits, qualifying powered ultralights fall into four main design categories. These are Powered Paragliders (Paramotors), Powered Parachutes (PPCs), Weight-Shift Control Trikes, and Fixed-Wing Ultralights. Powered Paragliders are the lightest and most portable of the categories and generally consist of a backpack motor unit and a ram-air fabric wing. The motor typically weighs around 46–65 lb (21–29 kg).

    Sources indicate that powered Parachutes are wheeled carts that carry a small two-stroke or four-stroke engine suspended under a large, square parachute canopy. These designs provide a very slow flight speed and high stability. Weight-Shift Control Trikes are a type of minimalist hang-glider-style wing mounted above a lightweight three-wheeled carriage. These are steered in pitch and roll by shifting the center of gravity rather than using traditional flight control surfaces.

    Industry observers note that fixed-Wing Ultralights are the closest category to a conventional aircraft and resemble traditional miniature aircraft. They are lightweight, low-speed recreational airplanes with rigid wings and conventional three-axis flight controls (ailerons, elevator, and rudder). These aircraft are designed for affordable, accessible sport and leisure flying. U-Fly-It Aerolite 103 (discussed below) makes some aircraft that fit into this category.

    In a recent development, the FAA stipulates that ultralight operations can only be conducted as a sporting or recreational activity. The operators of the vehicles are responsible for assessing risk and ensuring their own safety. The FAA also cautions, "the ultralight community is encouraged to adopt good operation practices and programs in order to avoid more extensive regulation by the Federal Aviation Administration.".

    It has been revealed that in the US, ultralights can be purchased through specialized dealers, manufacturers, and classified marketplaces such as Barnstormers, Hangar67, and PilotMix. Examples of ultralights on the market include the Northwing ATF Trike, Northwing Maverick Ultralight, Aero-Tech 2000 Lockwood Drifter, and U-Fly-It Aerolite 103. The prices of ultralights vary considerably on the marketplace. Second-hand examples can cost a few thousand dollars; newly introduced craft may cost up to tens of thousands.

    U-Fly-It Aerolite 103 says of its products, "The Aerolite 103 Quick-Build Kit has one of the lowest assembly times in the industry. Average for a first time builder is approximately 30-40 hours, and experienced builders can assemble the aircraft in less than 30 hours." It also advertises its Complete Aerolite 103 Quick-Build Airframe Kit at a price of $19,450. Customers have the choice of having the kit assembled through a dealer for an extra fee.

    According to recent reports, it should be noted that the information above is regulated by the FAA, and the FAA only has jurisdiction in US airspace. None of this is binding in other countries, and other countries have different sets of rules and regulations. In some cases, other countries are more generous with their allowances than the US, and in other cases, they are more restrictive. That mentioned, all other peer countries are more restrictive in the sense that pilots must uniformly have some sort of basic license or registration.

    Among countries like Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, Newly introduced Zealand, and Europe, the United States appears to be the only country that does not require a pilot license/permit or ultralight registration. At the same time, the minimum ultralight category in some countries can be much heavier than in the US. In Canada, it's 1,200 lb (544 kg MTOW), while it's 661 lb (300 kg) in the United Kingdom.

    Some countries (e.g., Australia, Newly introduced Zealand, Europe/EASA) may allow the aircraft to be two-seaters, although the conditions in which a passenger can be carried vary. New Zealand and Australia take a self-administration approach rather than direct government licensing. In Australia, it is controlled under Civil Aviation Order 95.10 and 95.55, and in New Zealand CAA Part 103, with New Zealand borrowing FAA numbering.

    The next step up from a Part 103 ultralight in the United States is the FAA Sport Pilot Certificate (governed by 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart J). The FAA created two upcoming pilot certificates in 2004 to enable pilots to operate aircraft that meet specific criteria without the need for a medical certificate. Those certificates were Sport Pilot and Flight Instructor with a Sport Pilot Rating. The Sport Pilot rule was massively expanded by the FAA's MOSAIC final rule, which went into effect in October 2025.

    Under these updated rules, light sport aircraft no longer have a 1,320 lb (598 kg) weight limit. The weight limit has been abolished. Under MOSAIC, a light-sport category airplane is permitted to have up to four seats and a VS0 stall of 61 knots or less (14 CFR 22.100). A sport pilot may fly any airplane with a VS1 of 59 knots or less and up to four seats (14 CFR 61.316).

    Other regulations include that the cabin must be non-pressurized, it can't have multiple engines, and it must have fixed landing gear. However, sport pilots can now fly retractable landing gear and manually controllable-pitch propellers after receiving specific ground/flight training and an instructor endorsement. Obtaining a Sport Pilot Certificate requires 20 hours total, or half the minimum 40 hours for a Private Pilot.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Latino voters moved sharply away from Republicans this year, and a record number of Latino Democratic candidates were elected.
    • Sánchez has a warning for her fellow Democrats.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, california Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, here at a 2020 news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center, is the chair of BOLD PAC. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Latino voters moved sharply away from Republicans this year, and a record number of Latino Democratic candidates were elected.

    But California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez has a warning for her fellow Democrats.

    “Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” remarked Sánchez, who leads the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.

    Failure to address rising costs and push back against President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda could once again scramble the political calculus and spark another realignment in two years, said House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar of California.

    “While Latinos shifted towards Democrats and … gave us this mandate as a party, Democrats must continue to earn their trust, not just every two years, but every single day,’’ he noted.

    Sources indicate that leaders of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus joined newly elected Latino members on Tuesday for a news conference to celebrate the recent wins and the role the group played in securing the House majority for Democrats. The caucus will boast 55 members in the next Congress, its largest roster ever, according to Sánchez.

    BOLD PAC, the caucus’ campaign arm, invested heavily in Latino candidates this year, including in primaries.

    California Rep. Salud Carbajal noted that BOLD PAC raised more than $18.5 million this cycle, which helped candidates leverage outside money.

    Working-class majority-Latino districts in South Texas, Arizona and California were among the areas that provided Democrats with their biggest wins. Democrats capitalized on voter dissatisfaction over rising costs, the very concern that helped Trump and the GOP make significant gains among Hispanic voters just two years earlier.

    But the wins weren’t limited to districts with sizable Latino populations.

    Rep.-elect Denise Powell, who flipped a swing seat in Nebraska, credited BOLD PAC for playing a key role in her win.

    Sources indicate that “Yes, there are Latinos in Omaha, and those Latinos actually helped decide this race,’’ she mentioned. “BOLD believed in me as a candidate, but they also believed in our community.”.

    Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido, who came to politics after a successful career as a Latin Grammy-winning Tejano singer, flipped a redrawn South Texas border district that Trump would have carried by 18 points in 2024.

    “A lot of people feel like they don't belong to either party. But there's one thing about Latinos is we belong to each other,’’ Pulido stated. “It's very hard to be a Latino right now in this country. … I expect to see us united, more united than ever, because it's a tough time right now.”.

    Industry observers note that several of the winning candidates deployed novel strategies to reach voters. Pulido famously began performing at quinceañeras after his Republican opponent dismissed him as a performer.

    In a recent development, colorado Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, who flipped a battleground district north of Denver, attended World Cup and Broncos watch parties. “If people don't hear our message, then it doesn't matter,’’ he said.

    The candidates “met those voters where they were,’’ Sánchez remarked. “They went into those communities and interacted in a very real and meaningful way. That's something I think that strategists or consultants don't always get. It's not just about pumping out lots of television commercials.”.

    According to recent reports, amid those successes for Latino Democrats, Florida, home to one of the largest Latino electorates in the country, was a different story. Republicans held all three majority-Latino districts in the Sunshine State, though former news anchor Eliott Rodriguez, the son of Cuban immigrants, came within half a percentage point of unseating GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar in a district that backed Trump by 15 points in 2024.

    According to recent reports, BOLD PAC did have a victory to celebrate in Florida, with Rep. Darren Soto, the deputy chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, narrowly prevailing in a district that Republicans redrew as one that no longer had a Latino majority.

    “The redistricting wars ended up failing because of the investment by BOLD PAC,’’ Soto said.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that last Friday we saw the worst disruption to air travel that we’ve seen in the United States in over 25 years, as air traffic shut down nationwide for over four hours.
    • The logical question is how something going wrong with the work of one contractor could cause our entire aviation ecosystem to shut down:.
    • Sources indicate that so, what’s actually going on here?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that last Friday we saw the worst disruption to air travel that we’ve seen in the United States in over 25 years, as air traffic shut down nationwide for over four hours. We promptly learned that this happened because L3Harris, a government contractor, was doing maintenance to switch telecommunications lines from copper to fiber.

    The logical question is how something going wrong with the work of one contractor could cause our entire aviation ecosystem to shut down:.

    Sources indicate that so, what’s actually going on here? A new report sheds some more light on this….

    CNN has some insights into how little oversight there was of the work being performed by FAA contractor L3Harris, which led to the ground stop disaster that we saw. When was oversight reduced? Well, in early 2025, coinciding with the FAA laying off a large number of employees, as part of Elon Musk’s “Department of Government Efficiency” (DOGE) stunt.

    Sources indicate that according to this report, last Friday morning, an FAA technician escorted a contractor from L3Harris into a remote radio communications site for air traffic control in southern Arkansas, to replace a decades-old router. The FAA technician’s belief was that his role was done once the contractor entered the facility, according to people familiar with what happened, plus the union representing FAA employees.

    That router replacement ended up being what triggered the communications challenges across the country, ultimately leading to the nationwide ground stop.

    FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford insists that the L3Harris engineer performing the upgrade “was monitored by an FAA technician” and that a risk assessment was performed, but sources dispute that characterization, pointing out that the technician “was only there to unlock the door,” and that “there was no monitoring.”.

    Funny enough, an FAA spokesperson later contradicted Bedford, saying “the FAA escort is responsible for providing the L3Harris technician access to and from the building,” and “because it is L3 equipment, the escort is not there while the technician is doing work.” It’s amazing how they can’t even keep their narrative straight.

    This type of hands-off arrangement is apparently a recent development that happened under the Trump administration, and a change to how the FAA used to handle things. In March 2025, an FAA memo laid out changes to how FAA maintenance and upgrades would be carried out, in order to speed things up. The memo stated that “it is critical to approve maintenance performed by the Telecommunication Vendors without delay.”.

    With this policy, the FAA also went from receiving maintenance “requests” from private contractors that needed to be approved, to receiving “notifications” of intended work, noting that “this work will proceed without FAA approval,” if not processed in time.

    Sources indicate that while the memo claimed that an FAA liaison will evaluate the “purpose, severity, criticality and impact” of the work, there are reportedly only a handful of liaisons nationwide, processing thousands of notifications. In this case, L3Harris reportedly submitted its “notification” with just a few days notice, meaning there was no meaningful oversight.

    A spokesperson for the union representing FAA employees explains that “orders were to simply let the contractor in the building,” that he “had no direction to help or assist in any way,” and that “no PASS-represented employee was asked to conduct a risk assessment on this particular upgrade.”.

    It also has to be pointed out that the March 2025 memo about a reduction in oversight came just weeks after Elon Musk’s DOGE laid off hundreds of FAA employees, making for the biggest single year layoffs at the organization in history.

    That’s the beauty of slashing government inefficiency, right? If everything is working well, then we must not need all of those employees, eh? So to have a handful of people being “notified” of work and having to do an analysis sounds like it could be a problem.

A contractor with L3Harris was given access to a site to replace wiring, with virtually no oversight from an FAA employee.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Atmos Rewards is the loyalty program of Alaska and Hawaiian, and that includes three co-branded credit cards. There’s only one business credit card in the portfolio, and that’s the Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card.

    According to recent reports, along those lines, there’s a major upgrade, as the card has just undergone a full refresh. The bad news is that the card’s annual fee has gone up considerably (at least for most people), and the benefits have also changed. Let’s take a look, because as you’d expect, the changes are a mixed bag.

    The good news is that there’s a huge incentive to apply for the card, given the massive limited-time welcome bonus of 90,000 Atmos Rewards points after spending $6,000 within the first 90 days.

    Link: Learn more about the Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card.

    Sources indicate that the Atmos Rewards Business Card is undergoing some major updates. This includes a higher annual fee, new rewards structure, and new set of perks. However, these changes only apply to new card members, as existing card members will keep the old benefits (and fee).

    It has been revealed that let me emphasize that the card has a huge limited time welcome bonus of 90,000 Atmos Rewards points after spending $6,000 within the first 90 days. So that’s a major incentive to apply for the card, if you’re eligible. I value Atmos Rewards points at 1.5 cents each, so to me, that’s worth $1,350.

    With that out of the way, let’s go over the details….

    According to recent reports, the Atmos Rewards Business Card now has a flat $195 annual fee, which covers the primary card member and any employee cards. Previously, the card had an annual fee of $70 per company, plus $25 per employee, so the minimum annual fee you’d pay would be $95.

    It goes without saying that this change represents a significant increase in the annual fee, unless you had more than four employee credit cards on your account.

    According to recent reports, the Atmos Rewards Business Card also has a new rewards structure. The card now offers:.

    According to recent reports, what has changed here is the new 10x points for booking through Atmos for Business (great for those who can use it), as well as a full overhaul of the 2x points categories. Previously the card offered 2x points on eligible gas, EV charging stations, shipping, and local transit purchases (including rideshare), while now it just offers 2x points on dining. As before, the card offers one status point for every $3 spent, with no cap.

    The Atmos Rewards Business Card is picking up quite a few new benefits that it didn’t previously offer:.

    The refreshed card also keeps a first checked bag free and preferred boarding on Alaska and Hawaiian flights for the card member and up to six guests on the same reservation when the trip is paid with the card, a 20% rebate on eligible inflight purchases, a 10% rewards bonus for cardholders with an eligible Bank of America small business account, and no foreign transaction fees.

    Let me emphasize that the card will no longer offer a $99 companion fare, so that’s being replaced by the new 50% off vouchers that can be earned with spending.

    As of November 18, 2026, customers who apply for a new Atmos Rewards Business Card will be receiving the refreshed card, with the new benefits and fee.

    It has been revealed that applications submitted before November 18 will continue under the prior card offering. What’s interesting is that current cardholders will keep their existing benefits, and will not be automatically moved over. However, you can call up Bank of America if you’d like to see about the opportunity of switching.

    As of now, it sounds like there are no intends to transition people to the newly introduced system, so existing card members shouldn’t be negatively impacted by this.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that on paper, a manufacturer's catalog sheet is a clean, reassuring place.
    • How, then, can an airline reconcile a theoretical $15 million list price with a $26.2 million standalone spare invoice, or, conversely, the steep 40% to 50% volume discounts that mega-fleets routinely extract during multi-year aircraft orders?
    • Recent findings suggest that according to market intelligence data from Safe Fly Aviation, a brand-newly introduced LEAP-1A or LEAP-1B carries a baseline catalog and market appraisal value ranging from $12 million to $18 million per unit.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that on paper, a manufacturer's catalog sheet is a clean, reassuring place. At the top of many engine valuation benchmarks, you will find the CFM LEAP, the exclusive powerplant for the Boeing 737 MAX and co-dominant engine on the Airbus A320neo family, pegged at a baseline market value of $12 million to $18 million per unit. But walk into a board meeting where a major carrier is acquiring standalone spare hardware, and that tidy catalog figure disappears entirely. In the case of EVA Air’s high-profile August 2026 acquisition, the Taiwanese carrier committed up to $131 million for a batch of just five spare LEAP-1A30S engines, translating to an effective outlay of roughly $26.2 million per engine once dedicated support packages and spare parts pools were factored into the contract.

    How, then, can an airline reconcile a theoretical $15 million list price with a $26.2 million standalone spare invoice, or, conversely, the steep 40% to 50% volume discounts that mega-fleets routinely extract during multi-year aircraft orders? Between GE Aerospace and Safran’s duopoly market leverage, surging supply chain inflation, and bleak maintenance realities like $4.5 million performance-restoration shop visits, the true cost of a CFM LEAP in 2026 is by no means a fixed price.

    Recent findings suggest that according to market intelligence data from Safe Fly Aviation, a brand-newly introduced LEAP-1A or LEAP-1B carries a baseline catalog and market appraisal value ranging from $12 million to $18 million per unit. With this considered, quoting this sticker price to an airline fleet manager is akin to citing the window sticker of a commercial airliner; it bears little resemblance to the actual transaction price.

    When major carriers place multi-decade fleet orders for A320neo or 737 MAX families, original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) like GE Aerospace and Safran use aggressive discounting structures. Through bundled airframe-and-engine packages and volume concessions, airlines routinely extract steep discounts of 40% to 50% or more, compressing actual net transaction prices down into the $7 million to $10 million range.

    In a recent development, conversely, when an operator steps outside a massive fleet order to purchase a standalone spare engine to protect its network against unexpected AOG (Aircraft on Ground) events, those volume discounts can disappear overnight. A clear example of this market reality emerged in August 2026, when EVA Air secured board approval to acquire five spare LEAP-1A30S engines for up to $131 million. As reported by Aviator.aero, that single transaction valued the hardware, spare parts pools, and technical support terms at roughly $26.2 million per engine unit.

    Sources indicate that the stark pricing divergence, ranging from a subsidized $8 million fleet cost to a $26.2 million standalone spare premium, begins to show how CFM International and lessors manage asset valuation. The key point is, however, that specific variant ratings and aerodynamic architectures, such as the LEAP-1A versus the LEAP-1B, alter these baseline valuations on the global market.

    Industry observers note that the core engineering philosophy is shared across the family, but the market valuation diverges sharply between the LEAP-1A, which powers the A320neo family in a duopoly market alongside Pratt & Whitney’s GTF, and the LEAP-1B, which has a sole-source monopoly powering every 737 MAX. According to technical appraisals from ISTAT and manufacturer structural guidelines, these mechanical and competitive divergences directly dictate how lessors and airlines price each variant.

    Recent findings suggest that each distinction carries heavy economic consequences for operators managing asset portfolios. The larger 78-inch fan (198.12 centimeters) and higher thrust profile of the LEAP-1A require distinct nacelle integration and pylon interfaces, while the LEAP-1B's tighter 69-inch (175.26 centimeters) geometry was custom-engineered to fit the lower-slung ground clearance of the 737 airframe design. Consequently, market liquidity and residual value curves behave differently for each variant, influencing how lessors structure spare pools and long-term financing.

    It has been revealed that the reality is that acquiring the hardware is just the opening chapter of a twenty-year financial commitment. Once these powerplants are hung beneath narrowbody wings across global networks, maintenance contracts and long-term rate-per-flight-hour agreements begin to shape airline balance sheets.

    Getting those all-notable hardware delivery slots is just the beginning of a financial commitment that spans decades. Once a narrowbody aircraft enters commercial service, the acquisition ledger gives way to relentless operational cash burn driven by maintenance reserves and Rate Per Flight Hour (RPFH) agreements. According to 2026 MRO benchmarks published by Safe Fly Aviation, airline treasurers swiftly discover that the sticker price accounts for only a fraction of an engine's total cost of ownership.

    According to recent reports, operating a CFM LEAP powerplant incurs ongoing maintenance reserve contributions ranging from $350 to $600 per flight hour, a substantial escalation compared to the mature CFM56-7B benchmark of $200 to $350 per flight hour. When these powerplants finally cycle into MRO facilities for heavy maintenance, full performance-restoration visits demand anywhere from $3,000,000 to $4,500,000+ per event, as noted in Simple Flying analysis.

    That heavy capital outlay is heavily influenced by the incorporation of advanced high-pressure turbine (HPT) durability kits and module replacements, dwarfing the $1,500,000 to $3,500,000 overhaul baseline typical of older CFM generation powerplants.

    In a recent development, to mitigate these cash-flow shocks, CFM International offers structured dollar-per-engine-flight-hour pricing programs designed to lock in cost predictability. But even with structured support agreements in place, operators still have to deal with escalating shop visit turnaround times and rigorous technical upgrades.

    It has been revealed that the economic reality of operating a narrowbody fleet in 2026 cannot be separated from the intensive engineering interventions needed to keep modern high-bypass powerplants on wing. While the CFM LEAP delivers a 15% reduction in fuel burn compared to the legacy CFM56, early-generation engines operating in harsh, high-cycle environments faced accelerated thermal stress. As detailed in Simple Flying coverage and Aviation International News, issues such as fuel nozzle carbon coking, driven by post-shutdown thermal soak, and high-pressure turbine (HPT) stage shroud wear sent engines to maintenance visits way earlier than expected.

    It has been revealed that to combat these wear patterns, CFM International rolled out comprehensive maturity packages, including advanced HPT durability kits and the Reverse Bleed System (RBS) designed to circulate cooling air through the core after shutdown. By mid-2026, over 1,200 LEAP-1A durability kits had been deployed across global overhaul networks, while similar certification milestones progressed for the LEAP-1B.

    However, these mandatory retrofits and shop-visit inductions collided with wider aerospace supply chain problems. MRO turnaround times (TAT) stretched from historical windows of 60 to 90 days out to 120 to 180+ days, leaving over 100 aircraft temporarily engine-less worldwide and driving global spare engine leasing costs past historic ceilings.

    It has been revealed that the acute shortage of quick-turn spare engines and congested MRO slots made airline financial planners factor significant contingency buffers into their operating budgets. Ideally, no carrier wants to be dealing with these aftermarket friction points, so a vital alternative strategy has taken center stage across fleet management circles.

    When MRO shop queues stretch for months, and spare parts are locked in global backlogs, purchasing an extra engine outright becomes an unviable capital expenditure for many commercial carriers. Instead, airline financial planners increasingly turn to engine lessors like Willis Lease Finance and AerCap to secure short-term and long-term protection against unexpected Aircraft on Ground (AOG) events, as noted by Acumen Aviation.

    According to market intelligence reports from Safe Fly Aviation, monthly lease rates for next-generation narrowbody powerplants routinely exceed $130,000, reflecting the intense competition for serviceable assets in a supply-constrained environment.

    Leasing rather than purchasing shifts the financial burden from a heavy upfront balance-sheet liability to a predictable operating expense, protecting carriers from the cash-flow shocks of sudden maintenance visit inductions. Lessors absorb the long-term asset depreciation risks while managing complex maintenance reserves, allowing operators to scale their available engine pools up or down depending on seasonal network demands.

    According to recent reports, the growing reliance on engine leasing highlights how modern airline fleet management has evolved from simple hardware acquisition into dynamic portfolio optimization. Lessors and financial institutions now take on a larger share of narrowbody asset risk, and so the true economic value of a CFM LEAP is increasingly defined by its liquidity and lease-rate retention across its operating lifecycle.

    Ultimately, viewing a CFM LEAP engine through the narrow lens of a catalog sticker price or an isolated acquisition invoice misses the entire financial reality of modern narrowbody operations. Airlines balance upfront fleet discounts against twenty years of escalating maintenance reserves, rigorous durability retrofits, and soaring shop visit costs, so the true price of powering the world's most popular single-aisle jets is defined by lifecycle endurance.

    Industry observers note that the emergence of mature Used Serviceable Material (USM) streams and advanced hot-section upgrades is something that will look to establish a newly introduced economic baseline for narrowbody powerplants. Whether operating under a twenty-year rate-per-flight-hour agreement or navigating spot-market spare leases exceeding $130,000 monthly, airline financial planners must treat engine management as an active portfolio exercise rather than a passive capital expense. In an aviation market where margins are razor-thin, mastering the hidden costs of the LEAP engine separates profitable fleet expansion from grounding liabilities.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, citi Shop takes some of the work out of saving money online. Once you've installed its browser extension, it acts as a shopping portal and coupon hunter all-in-one, rewarding you with statement credits.

    Industry observers note that it has broad reach, too, with more than 5,000 participating online merchants. That's easier than a traditional online shopping portal, which requires you to remember to start at the portal and click through before filling your cart.

    Its ease of use makes it a great resource, but other portals or special discounts may save you more.

    Here's how Citi Shop works and what to consider to determine if it's the best savings path for you.

    Industry observers note that citi Shop is a free browser extension for primary cardholders with an eligible Citi credit card, including ThankYou points cards and cobranded cards. Citi retail and commercial cards are usually ineligible.

    Offers come as either a percentage back or a fixed amount back, and your earnings are applied as a statement credit on the Citi card you selected during enrollment.

    Citi Shop is separate from Citi Merchant Offers, which requires you to enroll in targeted offers with a specific Citi card and then use that card for the qualifying purchase.

    Both Citi Shop and traditional portals give you an extra reward for making purchases they track.

    But Citi Shop brings potential rebates to you, rather than requiring you to initiate your savings search. The extension automatically displays a pop-up with an available offer when you visit a participating website. You'll have the option to activate the offer before checkout.

    All of Citi Shop's rebates are provided as statement credits, unlike the potential airline miles, hotel points or credit card rewards of traditional portals.

    What I like about Citi Shop is that it also acts like a shopping assistant. Instead of opening six coupon sites only to discover that every code expired last Tuesday, it handles the scavenger hunt for you and tests available promo codes on your behalf.

    Recent findings suggest that like Capital One Shopping, Citi Shop uses a browser extension. However, Capital One Shopping doesn't require a Capital One card to enroll and its rewards can be redeemed for eligible gift cards instead of a statement credit.

    Sources indicate that generally speaking, Citi Shop clashes with other shopping portals. Both work by referring and tracking your purchase, so they can be mutually exclusive. You'll need to make your purchase through whichever offer is better.

    Related: Chase shopping portal guide: How to earn bonus Ultimate Rewards points.

    Sources indicate that unless Citi Shop finds a promo code, it won't lower your total at checkout. Its returns arrive later as statement credits and may require patiently waiting two to six months, sometimes longer.

    According to recent reports, even though you need an eligible Citi card to enroll, you don’t have to pay with it. Citi allows any payment method accepted by the merchant.

    I really appreciate the flexibility to choose the best card for each purchase. For electronics, I might pick a card with an extended warranty while I might stick to a travel rewards credit card for hotel bookings. You can even pay with a gift card if you wish.

    Regardless of how you pay, the statement credit will post to the Citi card you enrolled.

    If you have an eligible Citi card but rarely remember to click through a shopping portal, Citi Shop is an easy win. Install it, activate offers when the pop-up appears and let the credits come to you. That convenience can also be a substantial benefit if you have partners or other family members who aren't as motivated to strategize on rewards as you are.

    But with a little extra effort, you might be able to earn even more. When the Citi Shop pop-up appears with an offer, take a minute to compare before you click Activate.

    Checking a shopping portal aggregator such as Cashback Monitor shows payouts from multiple cash-back, airline and credit card portals, making it easier to compare a Citi Shop statement credit with points or miles elsewhere.

    Suppose a $200 jacket is marked down to $160. Citi Shop finds a $10 coupon, bringing the checkout price to $150, and offers 8% back. Assuming the full amount qualifies, you'd receive a $12 Citi Shop credit. If you pay with a card that earns 2% back and has an activated merchant offer for $5 off a $100 purchase, you'd collect another $8. After all the credits and rewards post, your net cost would be $130.

    Industry observers note that read the terms before getting too excited. Some brands, products, gift cards or coupon codes may be excluded and you might not be able to stack every layer every time. Still, you can often use multiple discounts simultaneously for a better deal.

    Citi Shop is not a program for instant gratification. Citi says statement credits post 61 to 180 days after a completed purchase, though some can take longer.

    Industry observers note that in many cases, offers may show as pending long before they officially pay out, to account for potential returns. Hotel rewards may remain pending until after the stay. Eventually, you'll see it on your statement as "CITI SHOP STATEMENT CREDIT.".

    According to recent reports, if a credit hasn't posted after the expected window, contact Citi using the number on the back of your enrolled card. You may want to keep good records along the way, like a screenshot of the offer and an e-receipt from the purchase.

    In a recent development, citi Shop's biggest advantage is convenience. It does the heavy lifting by reminding you to activate offers so you don't miss out on earnings from your online orders, while testing coupon codes along the way. The offers themselves may or may not be the highest available, but they are certainly the easiest.

    To truly optimize your returns, you'll want to compare Citi Shop earnings with those from other shopping portals — and stack other forms of saving along the way. But when that sounds like too much, the ease of this extension can still be a great way to tack on some extra returns.

    Jeffries puts immigration bill high on Democratic priority list

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (734 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday.
    • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move swiftly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.
    • Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move swiftly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.

    Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.

    Recent findings suggest that “One of the things that we need to do is to move the Dream and Promise Act for DACA recipients and TPS recipients,” Jeffries said, referring to a Democratic bill introduced last year. “We should actually move that bill immediately.”.

    The proposal aims to create a path to citizenship for certain Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipients and Temporary Protected Status holders. Similar legislation has been a top priority for Democrats in both chambers for more than a decade, with Democrats unable to advance this bill in the House while Republicans have held the majority.

    Jeffries also reiterated his calls to rein in Immigration and Customs Enforcement and redirect funding allocated to the agency through Republicans' budget law known as the One Major Beautiful Bill Act, while expressing a desire for bipartisan cooperation on immigration more broadly.

    In a recent development, “We think the border should be safe and strong and secure, and we think our immigration system overall is broken,” Jeffries said. “We need to fix it in a comprehensive way, and certainly, it's our hope that a handful of Republicans will be willing to join us, so we can fix it in a bipartisan way.”.

    Recent findings suggest that on healthcare, however, Jeffries offered fewer specifics, suggesting Democrats still have decisions to make before taking control of the chamber. Democrats broadly agree on the need to restore subsidies for plans purchased through health insurance markets that expired at the end of 2025. But the question of what additional steps the party should pursue with the goal of expanding coverage and lowering prices is likely to be a major test of Democratic leadership’s ability to find consensus among its robust upcoming majority.

    When asked how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that's all part of an ongoing conversation.”.

    The Newly introduced York Democrat outlined several broader healthcare priorities, including reversing Medicaid cuts enacted under President Donald Trump, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, all of which Democrats have vowed to do over the last year.

    “Out of the gate, what we clearly have to do is fix our broken healthcare system in terms of the damage that's been done by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists over the last two years, and that clearly involves reversing the Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits, and beginning to engage in supporting medical research, particularly things like research for pediatric cancer,” Jeffries added.

    Democrats established a healthcare working group earlier this Congress, led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. and Terri Sewell, D-Ala., to gather perspectives and develop policy proposals as the party works toward a broader agenda.

    In a recent development, without an unveiled challenger, Jeffries has expressed confidence that he’ll secure the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who have mentioned they remain “undecided” ahead of Wednesday’s elections. Jeffries, who was introduced as “Speaker Jeffries” on election night, said last week he was “very confident we’ll get there” and confirmed that the caucus will hold a recorded vote in the contest.

    Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to go forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives, many aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

    Jeffries noted Tuesday the approach mirrors the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who is best positioned to lead based on “track record, experience and vision.”.

    In a recent development, this report was corrected to reflect Rep. Nancy Pelosi’s status as a current member.

    Finnair Celebrates International Men’s Day With All-Male Crew On Flight

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (960 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • There’s still quite a gender gap in the airline industry, with a disproportionate number of pilots being male, and a disproportionate number of flight attendants being female.
    • Today is (apparently) International Men’s Day.
    • The crew consisted of 10 people, comprised of two pilots and eight flight attendants.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    There’s still quite a gender gap in the airline industry, with a disproportionate number of pilots being male, and a disproportionate number of flight attendants being female. Airlines will sometimes have special celebrations with all-female crews, so here’s an interesting twist on that.

    Today is (apparently) International Men’s Day. We often see airlines commemorate International Women’s Day, but there aren’t many airlines that celebrate the equivalent for men… well, except Finnair! The airline has today operated its annual flight with an all-male crew. This was the case for Finnair flight AY1331, from Helsinki (HEL) to London (LHR), using an Airbus A350-900.

    The crew consisted of 10 people, comprised of two pilots and eight flight attendants. The gate agents were also all men. So, why is this notable? Finnair highlights how only around 10% of cabin crew at the airline are male, but the company hopes to see that number grow in the future.

    I think this is a fun concept, and it would be nice to see a closer to 50/50 gender ratio in both the cockpit and cabin, as it would show that everyone is given a fair chance at such a career.

    I think it’s worth acknowledging that at many airlines, hiring of flight attendants is still primarily or exclusively based on gender. Now, the policies do vary significantly by airline, but perhaps an extreme example is India’s largest airline, IndiGo, which only hires female flight attendants. It’s literally written on the application, that it’s a job for “Female Indian nationals.”.

    It’s all so strange, because the airline has this super enthusiastic page about the importance of diversity in the workplace, and says “all employment decisions are made solely on the basis of merit and qualifications, without regard to a candidate’s gender…” You mean except the single largest portion of your workforce, which is cabin crew?

    Sources indicate that what’s interesting is that while those gender restrictions exist in the cabin, roughly 18% of the carrier’s pilots are female, which is way above the global average of 7%. That’s obviously a conscious effort, so I guess the idea is that women can become pilots but men can’t become flight attendants.

    In a recent development, in fairness, I suspect part of the motivation here is that IndiGo flight attendants share hotel rooms on layovers, and that is a bit more complicated with mixed genders. Then again, it seems easy enough to just try to pair male flight attendants on trips, so it’s hardly a hurdle that can’t be overcome.

    In a recent development, while we’re used to seeing airlines celebrate International Women’s Day, it’s rare to see an airline celebrating International Men’s Day. Finnair has operated an all-male flight today, intended to highlight how only 10% of flight attendants at the airline are male, and the airline wants to change that. While an unconventional initiative nowadays, I think this is still pretty cool.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Dad, here’s a blog post you should pay attention to (and thanks to Steve for flagging this)….
    • With banks, it’s typically possible to get your account statements by email or mail.
    • We’re making the switch to paperless billing statements and account communications, beginning February 2027.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Dad, here’s a blog post you should pay attention to (and thanks to Steve for flagging this)….

    With banks, it’s typically possible to get your account statements by email or mail. There’s no denying that consumer preferences have shifted over the years, and along those lines, Amex has just sent an email to card members, informing them that “we’re making the switch to paperless.” Here’s the main part of the email:.

    We’re making the switch to paperless billing statements and account communications, beginning February 2027.

    Here’s what happens nextWe want to help you get ready to make the switch too. So, we’ve enrolled your account listed above in the paperless delivery option – but for now, we’ll continue to send you communications about your account in the mail. We’ll also mail your billing statements for the closing dates of November 2026, December 2026, and January 2027.

    Recent findings suggest that after that, we’ll send account communications to you by email, and you’ll receive your monthly billing statements electronically. When they’re ready, you’ll be able to view them anytime by logging in to your account online at americanexpress.com or in the American Express App.

    Recent findings suggest that now, that makes it sound like people will be forced to switch to paperless billing, but I don’t believe that’s actually the case? Because further down in the email, it indicates this:.

    According to recent reports, not ready to go paperless? No problem! You can re-enroll in paper billing statements and account communications by going to americanexpress.com/paperlesssettings, selecting “U.S. Mail,” and following the prompts to opt back in.

    So it seems like what’s happening here is that Amex will try to force everyone into paperless billing by making it the default, but maybe those who specifically once again state their preferences for paper billing will be able to maintain that communication method?

    Suffice it to say that going back 25 years, a vast majority of people got paper statements for their credit cards, while nowadays a vast majority of people get paperless statements, obviously reflecting the shift we’ve seen in how the internet is used.

    It’s funny, because I’m sure 99% of OMAAT readers would be confused at the thought of getting paper bills, and would wonder what purpose that serves. But then there are also people like my dad, who rely on paper statements for their credit cards, pay their statement by phone, etc.

    It has been revealed that so it does sound like people will have the option of opting back into paper billing after being auto-enrolled in paperless billing, so the concept isn’t being eliminated altogether. Still, for my dad, there would likely be quite the learning curve.

    Then again, up until less than a decade ago he didn’t have a cell phone and insisted he didn’t need one, while now he kind of loves it, for everything from texting, to Googling all kinds of stuff. That’s of course a double-edged sword as well, because he seems to believe that if the Google AI summary states something, it must be true. We’re not talking things like vaccines. Instead, we’re talking things like whether the salmon at Red Lobster is good, etc. Anyway, I digress….

    As of February 2027, Amex will be automatically moving those with paper billing to paperless billing. While the message makes it sound like people will be forced to switch to paperless billing, that doesn’t seem to be the case, as Amex is also telling people they can once again enroll in paper billing statements and account communications if they’re “not ready to go paperless.” So Amex just seems to be trying to thin the ranks here of those using this feature.

    What do you make of Amex’s switch to paperless billing?

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s.
    • To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet presently consists of 25 planes, including:.
    • Aeromexico is planning on fully overhauling the premium cabins on these planes, as was confirmed by the manufacturer’s CEO at this week’s APEX FTE EXPO 2026.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s. This is interesting on many levels — we’ll see the larger Dreamliners get all-newly introduced business class cabins plus premium economy for the first time, we’ll see the smaller Dreamliners get the old business class cabins of the bigger Dreamliners, and we’ll see the airline adopt some Delta-style branding.

    To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet presently consists of 25 planes, including:.

    Aeromexico is planning on fully overhauling the premium cabins on these planes, as was confirmed by the manufacturer’s CEO at this week’s APEX FTE EXPO 2026.

    The plan is for the 787-9s to get all-new cabins, and in the process, the 787-8s will get the old business class seats from the 787-9s. That means the 787-8s will get reverse herringbone seats, which are still competitive, but of course not cutting edge (though still a huge improvement over the pairs of seats presently on the planes).

    Sources indicate that the 787-9s will really become the next-generation flagship planes for the airline, though some patience will be required. The expectation is that the first of these Dreamliners will be retrofitted in the next 18 to 24 months (so hopefully by some point in 2028), and then it’ll likely take a couple of years for the fleet to be upgraded.

    In a recent development, we’ll talk more about the latest business class product as such in a bit, but the idea is that the 787-9s will get business class suites, including a front row “business class plus” product. On top of that, the 787-9s will be getting a premium economy cabin for the first time.

    According to recent reports, the plane will also have up to 70% more premium seats than before. Presently, Aeromexico’s 787-9s have 36 business class seats, while the retrofitted planes will have a total of 61 premium seats, between business class and premium economy. So I suspect the business class cabin won’t actually get that much bigger, but instead, most of that premium addition will come in the form of the new premium economy cabin.

    It’s also worth mentioning that Aeromexico is adopting some Delta-style branding, as Delta owns a 20% stake in Aeromexico, and the two airlines have a close partnership.

    Aeromexico’s newly introduced premium products will be known as Premier One Suites Plus (the “business class plus” product), Premier One Suites (business class), and Premier (premium economy). It seems the 787-8 business class will just be branded as Premier One, given the lack of suites with doors. That all sure seems to be inspired by the Delta One branding that’s used by the carrier’s partner.

    Seth Miller from PaxEx.Aero flags how Aeromexico’s latest Boeing 787-9 business class suite is from Recaro, as the airline is reportedly the launch customer for this new product. However, the exact product hasn’t actually been named.

    According to recent reports, aeromexico CEO Dr. Andres Conesa unveiled the carrier's new premium economy cabin plus refreshed business class seat at #APEXFTEExpo in Singapore this week.Full teaser video in the story: paxex.aero/first-look-a….#PaxEx$RTX.

    I believe this might be an evolution of the Recaro R7 product (LATAM’s newest 787 business class), which in and of itself was already an evolution of the Recaro CL6720 product (Iberia’s newest A350 business class).

    It seems that what was unveiled earlier this year was the new Recaro R7 Horizon concept, which is the same idea, but with upgraded technology and customization.

    I imagine that we’ll learn more in the coming months, as this was an unusual way to unveil a newly introduced product. But this does seem to be officially happening, so it’s something to look forward to… down the road.

    According to recent reports, aeromexico is planning some big upgrades to its Dreamliners. The Boeing 787-9s will be getting all-upcoming cabins, including new business class suites, plus a premium economy cabin for the first time. There will even be a premium business product in the first row, with the products marketed as Premier One Suites Plus, Premier One Suites, and Premier.

    As this happens, the 787-8s will be getting the old reverse herringbone seats from the 787-9s, so that will be a meaningful upgrade as well. You can expect these latest cabins to roll out starting at some point in 2028, so some patience will be required. I can’t wait to learn more!
